pages.title: Introduction
pages.summary: What NetFlow9 is, what you can build with it, and how these docs are organized.
pages.html:
NetFlow9 is a workflow automation platform. You draw a workflow on a canvas: a trigger that starts it, and steps connected one after another. NetFlow9 runs it for you each time the trigger fires: on a schedule, when an email or a web request arrives, when someone fills in a form or uploads a file, or when you press Run.

What you can build

A few examples of what teams automate with NetFlow9:

  • Email processing: read the messages that arrive in a mailbox, pick out the order number or the attachment, store them in a data table and reply.
  • Approvals: a form starts the workflow, a Human task asks a manager to approve or reject, and the workflow continues with the answer.
  • Integrations: call any HTTP API, move files over FTP / SFTP, work with Google Drive, Sheets, Gmail and Calendar, or Microsoft 365 (Outlook, OneDrive / SharePoint, Excel, Teams).
  • AI steps: summarize, classify or extract data with Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, or a model you run yourself (Ollama, Lemonade).
  • Scheduled jobs: every night, fetch a report, compare it with yesterday's and send the differences by email.

The main parts

PartWhat it is for
Workflow designerThe canvas where you add steps, connect them and set them up. It saves as you work and shows errors before you run.
TriggersWhat starts a workflow: Manual, Schedule, Webhook, Form, File upload, Email (inbound).
StepsThe actions and the logic: If, Switch, Loop, Merge, Set, Wait, Code, HTTP Request, emails, data tables, human tasks, AI and the integrations.
Credentials & variablesThe passwords, API keys and OAuth connections the steps use, and the project's shared values. They are kept encrypted, so they never appear in a workflow.
Data tablesSimple tables inside NetFlow9 that workflows read and write, without a database of your own.
Forms and My tasksThe pages where people take part in workflows: they fill in forms and complete the tasks assigned to them.
Executions and logsEvery run: its state, a log of what each step did, the variables and the error, if any.

How these docs are organized

  • Getting started: the concepts and a first workflow, built step by step.
  • Building workflows: the designer, every trigger and step, expressions, errors, publishing and executions.
  • Workspace: forms, tasks, data tables, files, credentials and variables, the Assistant.
  • Account administration: users, roles, sign-in (MFA, LDAP, SAML), usage and the audit logs.
  • Self-hosting: installing and running NetFlow9 on your own server.
  • Developers: webhooks, the MCP server, the expression language and plugins.

Tip: press / anywhere on this site to search.

Next steps

Read Core concepts for the vocabulary, then build your first workflow in the Quick start.

pages.title: Core concepts
pages.summary: Accounts, projects, workflows, triggers, steps, variables, versions and executions: the vocabulary of NetFlow9.
pages.html:
This page explains the words used everywhere in NetFlow9 and in these docs. Each concept has its own page later on. This is the short version.

Account

An account is your organization in NetFlow9: a company or a team. It holds the users, the projects and everything in them. Its settings, such as the date formats, sign-in rules and how long logs are kept, apply to all of its users. The account's plan may set limits, such as the number of data tables, the space for files and the monthly AI credits, and which integrations are available. Account settings covers the settings, and Usage and AI credits the plan's limits.

Users and roles

Every person who signs in is a user of the account. What a user may do comes from their role. A new account has three roles:

  • Owner: everything, including the account's settings, users and roles.
  • Member: works in the projects they belong to: builds and runs workflows, manages credentials, tables and files.
  • Participant: takes part in workflows without building them: fills in the forms and completes the tasks assigned to them.

An owner can create more roles with their own permissions.

Projects

A project groups related work: its workflows, credentials and variables, data tables and files. A project has an owner and members, each with a role in the project. Only members see a project's content. Switch between projects from the project name at the top of the sidebar.

Workflows

A workflow is an automation: a trigger and the steps that follow it, drawn in the designer. A workflow has exactly one trigger. Every other step must be reachable from it.

Triggers

The trigger is the first step and decides when the workflow runs:

TriggerStarts a run
Manual TriggerWhen you press Run in the designer.
Schedule TriggerAt set times: every few minutes, daily, on certain weekdays…
WebhookWhen another system sends an HTTP request to the workflow's address.
FormWhen someone submits the workflow's form.
File uploadWhen a file is uploaded to the workflow.
Email (inbound)When an email arrives at the workflow's address.

To process a mailbox regularly, start with a Schedule Trigger followed by a Read emails (IMAP), Gmail or Outlook Mail step.

Steps and connections

A step does one thing: sends an email, calls an API, tests a condition, waits. Steps are connected from an output to the input of the next step. Most steps have one output. Some have several, and the run continues only on the matching one:

  • If has a true and a false output.
  • Switch has one output per case.
  • Steps that call other systems can have an error output, so a failure takes another path instead of stopping the run.

Loop repeats the steps inside it for each item of a list. Merge joins branches: it continues once all of them arrived, or at the first one. A Note is a comment on the canvas and is not connected.

Variables and expressions

Steps pass data to each other through variables. A step that produces something stores it in a variable. For example, HTTP Request stores the response in response by default, and a Set step stores the value you give it. Later steps read variables with expressions written between double braces:

Order {{ order.number }} from {{ mail.from }}
{{ response.body.items.length }}
{{ customer.name.toUpperCase() }}

A field that holds only one expression keeps the value's type (a number, a list, an object). Otherwise the result is text. The designer suggests the variables available at each step as you type. Expressions has the details.

Credentials and project variables

Credentials hold what steps need to connect to other systems: passwords, API keys, OAuth connections to Google or Microsoft, SMTP and IMAP servers. They belong to a project and are stored encrypted. A step only refers to a credential by name, so exporting or sharing a workflow never exposes a secret.

Project variables are shared values, such as a base URL or a team's email address. Any workflow of the project reads them as {{ vars.name }}.

Drafts, publishing and versions

What you edit in the designer is the workflow's draft. Its changes are saved automatically. A draft runs only when you press Run: the trigger does not start it.

Publishing saves the draft as a numbered version (v1, v2…) and makes it the one the trigger runs. You can keep editing the draft without affecting the published version, then publish again when ready. You can always see older versions, publish one again, or copy it back into the draft. Unpublishing stops the trigger from starting new runs.

Executions

Each run of a workflow is an execution. It records the version it ran, what started it (for example the webhook request or the email), the variables, and the state of every step:

StateMeaning
RunRunning now.
SleepWaiting: for a Wait step's time, or for a human task to be completed.
CompletedFinished without errors.
ErrorA step failed, and the error message says which and why.

The Executions panel in the designer lists a workflow's runs. For each run it shows the state, the error if any, the log (what each step did) and the variables. The account's execution log keeps a record of all runs.

pages.title: Quick start: your first workflow
pages.summary: Build, run and publish a workflow that calls a web API, checks the answer and stores a value.
pages.html:
In about ten minutes you will build a workflow that calls a web API, checks the answer and stores a value from it. You will run it from the designer, then see how to make it run by itself.

Before you start: sign in to NetFlow9 with a user that can create workflows in a project, such as an Owner or a Member of the project.

1. Create the workflow

  1. In the sidebar, next to Workflows, click +.
  2. The new workflow opens in the designer. To give it a name, click the gear icon in the toolbar, type My first workflow and save.

The canvas is empty, with a + button in the middle: "Add the first step: a trigger starts the workflow".

2. Add a trigger

  1. Click the + in the middle of the canvas. The step list opens, with a search box.
  2. Type manual and choose Manual Trigger.

A Manual Trigger has no settings: it starts a run when you press Run. It is the easiest trigger to try things with.

3. Call a web API

  1. Click the small + next to the trigger's output and choose HTTP Request. The new step is connected to the trigger, and its settings open.
  2. Set Method to GET and URL to https://httpbin.org/json. This public test API answers with a small JSON document.
  3. Leave Response variable as response, and close the settings.

When this step runs, response holds the answer: response.ok, response.status (200 when all went well), response.headers and response.body. JSON bodies are decoded, so you can reach into them with dots.

4. Check the answer

  1. Click the + next to the HTTP Request's output and choose If.
  2. In the first condition, set Test to {{ response.status }}, the operator to equals and Value to 200.

The If step now has two outputs, true and false. The run continues on the one that matches.

5. Store a value

  1. Click the + next to the If's true output and choose Set.
  2. Set Variable to title, and Value to {{ response.body.slideshow.title }}. As you type after {{, the designer suggests the variables available here.

Your workflow now reads: Manual Trigger → HTTP Request → If → (true) Set.

Note: the designer saves every change. The status at the right of the toolbar shows Saved. The bug icon opens the list of errors and warnings, such as a missing setting or a step that is not connected. A workflow with errors is saved, but it cannot be run or published until they are fixed.

6. Run it

  1. Click Run (the green play icon in the toolbar).
  2. The Executions panel opens at the bottom and shows the new run. It refreshes every few seconds while the run is in progress.
  3. When it is Completed, look at its Log (one line per step) and its Variables: response holds the API's answer, and title is Sample Slide Show.

If a step fails, the execution's state is Error, with the message of the step that failed. For example, change the URL to https://httpbin.org/status/404 and run again. The If now continues on its false output, because response.status is 404.

7. Make it run by itself

A Manual Trigger only runs when you press Run. To run the workflow automatically:

  1. Delete the Manual Trigger and add a Schedule Trigger in its place, for example every hour. Then connect its output to the HTTP Request's input.
  2. Open the status menu in the toolbar (it says Draft) and choose Publish the draft as v1. You can add a note about what changed.

The button turns green: v1 published. From now on the trigger starts a run every hour, and each run appears in the Executions panel. If you edit the workflow later, the draft is marked draft changed, while the trigger keeps running v1 until you publish again.

What next

  • Learn the canvas in The designer.
  • Browse the triggers and steps.
  • Store the API key of a real service in a credential, then use it in the HTTP Request.

pages.title: The designer
pages.summary: The canvas where you build a workflow: adding and connecting steps, their settings, saving, undo, and the panels.
pages.html:
Open a workflow from the sidebar (under Workflows) and it opens in the designer: a canvas with the workflow's steps and their connections, and a toolbar above it.

Note: the designer works best on a computer. On a phone you can still open, view and run a workflow.

The toolbar

ControlWhat it does
Errors / warnings badgesThe number of problems found in the workflow. Point at a badge to see the list.
Status menu (Draft, v3 published…)Publish, unpublish, versions, duplicate and delete. See Publishing and versions.
Zoom out / Fit / Zoom inThe canvas zoom. Fit shows the whole workflow.
Run (play icon)Runs the draft now. See Executions.
Executions (clock icon)Opens the panel with the workflow's runs.
Debug (bug icon)Opens the panel with the errors and warnings.
Settings (gear icon)The workflow's name and icon.
Undo / RedoSteps back and forward through your changes. Shortcuts: Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z (or Ctrl+Y).
Save statusSaved, Saving… or Not saved. Click it to retry a failed save.

Adding steps

  • The first step: on an empty canvas, click the + in the middle. A workflow starts with a trigger.
  • After a step: click the small + next to one of its outputs. The new step is placed to the right and already connected.
  • Anywhere: click the green + at the top left of the canvas to open the step list. Click a step to add it in the middle of the view, or drag it onto the canvas.

The step list has a search box: type part of a name, move with the arrow keys and press Enter to add the highlighted step, or Esc to close the list. A new step opens its settings right away.

Connecting steps

Drag from a step's output (on its right side) to another step's input (on its left side). To remove a connection, click it, then click the ✕ that appears in its middle.

Steps with several outputs show the name of each: true / false for If, the cases for Switch, success / error when a step continues on errors. An output may have several connections: the run then goes on along each of them.

Moving around

  • Drag the empty canvas to move the view. Use the mouse wheel to zoom, or pinch on a touch screen.
  • Drag a step by its body to move it. Drag its corner to resize it.
  • Click a step to select it. Press Delete or Backspace to delete the selected step, or use the trash icon on the step.

Step settings

Double-click a step, or use the pencil icon on it, to open its settings. The dialog is laid out the same way for every step:

  • On the first line: the step's name (shown on the canvas), the variable it sets, if any, and what happens on an error.
  • Then the credential and the operation, for steps that connect to other systems.
  • Then the step's own settings, with the limits and the timeout at the end.

Fields marked for expressions accept {{ }}. As you type after {{, the designer suggests the variables that exist at this point of the workflow, with their fields: for example response. suggests status, body, headers… See Expressions.

Steps that set a variable show its name on the canvas, under the title, so you can see where each variable comes from.

Saving

Every change is saved automatically a moment after you make it. You don't need a Save button: Ctrl+S only saves right away. If a save fails, for example when the connection drops, the designer tries again every few seconds and shows Not saved until it succeeds.

A draft is saved even when it has errors, such as a missing required setting. It cannot be run or published until they are fixed.

Errors and warnings

The designer checks the workflow as you build it:

  • Errors stop Run and Publish. Examples: The workflow has no trigger, Only one trigger is allowed, A trigger cannot be inside a loop, This step is connected to itself, and missing or invalid settings.
  • Warnings don't stop anything but point at likely mistakes, such as Not connected to the trigger or an expression that uses an unknown variable.

Open the Debug panel (bug icon) for the full list. Steps with a problem are marked on the canvas.

Loops on the canvas

A Loop is a box that holds other steps. Drag steps into it, or add them from an output of a step that is already inside. The steps inside run once for each item. The connection that leaves the loop's own output runs after the last item.

The Assistant

When the Assistant is enabled for your account, the designer has an Assistant panel. Describe what you want in plain words, such as "read new mails from the support mailbox and store the sender and subject in the Tickets table". The Assistant builds or changes the workflow on the canvas. See The Assistant.

pages.title: Triggers
pages.summary: What starts a workflow: Manual, Schedule, Webhook, Form, File upload and Email (inbound).
pages.html:
Every workflow starts with exactly one trigger. The trigger decides when the workflow runs, and puts what started it into a variable for the next steps: the request, the form's answers, the file, the email.

TriggerStarts a runVariable
Manual TriggerWhen you press Run in the designernone
Schedule TriggerAt set timesschedule_time
WebhookOn an HTTP request to the workflow's addresswebhook
FormWhen someone sends the workflow's formform, form_user
File uploadWhen a file is uploaded to the projectfile
Email (inbound)When an email arrives at the workflow's addressmail

Triggers run the published version

Except for the Manual Trigger, a trigger starts runs only while the workflow is published, and those runs use the published version, not the draft you are editing. Press Run to try the draft. See Publishing and versions.

Rules

  • A workflow has one trigger. To start the same steps in two ways, make two workflows.
  • A trigger has no input and cannot be placed inside a loop.
  • Every other step must be reachable from the trigger. Unreachable steps get a warning.

pages.title: Manual Trigger
pages.summary: Starts the workflow when you press Run in the designer.
pages.html:
The Manual Trigger starts a run when you press Run in the designer's toolbar. It has no settings and sets no variables. Use it while building and testing, and for workflows you only start by hand.

Run uses the draft, so you can try your latest changes without publishing.

Note: Run also works with a Schedule Trigger: it starts one run right away, without waiting for the schedule.

pages.title: Schedule Trigger
pages.summary: Runs the published workflow at set times: an interval, daily, weekly, monthly or a cron expression.
pages.html:
The Schedule Trigger runs the workflow at the times you set, as long as the workflow is published. The schedule uses the installation's time zone.

Settings

SettingDescription
RunChoices: At a regular interval; Every day; Every week; Every month; Advanced (cron expression). Default: Every day. Required.
EveryDefault: 15. (Shown for some values of Run.)
UnitsChoices: Minutes; Hours; Days. Default: Minutes. (Shown for some values of Run.)
OnChoices: Monday; Tuesday; Wednesday; Thursday; Friday; Saturday; Sunday. (Shown for some values of Run.)
AtDefault: 09:00. (Shown for some values of Run.)
On dayMonths without this day are skipped. Default: 1. (Shown for some values of Run.)
Cron expressionminute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, e.g. "30 8 * * 1-5" = weekdays at 08:30. (Shown for some values of Run.)

Examples

You wantSet
Every 15 minutesRun: At a regular interval, Every: 15, Units: Minutes
Every day at 07:30Run: Every day, At: 07:30
Monday and Thursday at 09:00Run: Every week, On: Monday, Thursday, At: 09:00
On the 1st of each monthRun: Every month, On day: 1
Weekdays at 08:30Run: Advanced, Cron: 30 8 * * 1-5

With Every month, months that don't have the chosen day are skipped. For example, day 31 skips April.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
schedule_timestringThe scheduled minute (ISO 8601)

Press Run in the designer to start one run right away, with the draft.

pages.title: Webhook
pages.summary: Starts the workflow when another system sends an HTTP request to the workflow's secret address.
pages.html:
A Webhook trigger gives the workflow its own address: https://<your NetFlow9>/hook/<token>. When another system sends an HTTP request to it, the published workflow runs with the request in a variable. The address is shown in the step's settings once the workflow is saved.

Warning: keep the address secret: anyone who has it can start the workflow. For more protection, set an Authentication method below.

Settings

SettingDescription
HTTP methodChoices: Any method; GET; POST; PUT; PATCH; DELETE. Default: POST. Required.
Content typeOf the request body (not checked for GET). Choices: Any; JSON (application/json); Web form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data); Plain text (text/*). Default: JSON (application/json). Required.
RespondChoices: When received (202, the workflow runs afterwards); When the workflow ends (200, with its state). Default: When received (202, the workflow runs afterwards). Required.
AuthenticationChoices: None (the secret URL only); Header with a secret value; Bearer token (Authorization: Bearer ...); Basic auth (username / password); HMAC-SHA256 signature of the body. Default: None (the secret URL only). Required.
Header nameHMAC: the header carries the hex signature (or sha256=<hex>). (Shown for some values of Authentication.)
Secret(Shown for some values of Authentication.)
Username(Shown for some values of Authentication.)
Password(Shown for some values of Authentication.)
Request variablee.g. {{ webhook.body }}, {{ webhook.query.id }}. Default: webhook. Required.

Authentication

MethodThe caller must send
NoneNothing: knowing the address is enough.
Header with a secret valueA header, named in Header name, with the Secret as its value.
Bearer tokenAuthorization: Bearer <secret>.
Basic authThe username and password (Authorization: Basic …).
HMAC-SHA256A header with the HMAC-SHA256 signature of the request body, keyed with the secret: hex, or sha256=<hex>. Many services (GitHub, Shopify, Stripe-like APIs) sign their webhooks this way.

A request that fails authentication gets 401 and starts nothing. A mode without its secret refuses every request.

The answer

  • When received (default): the caller gets 202 at once, with {"execution": "<id>", "state": "accepted"}. The workflow runs afterwards.
  • When the workflow ends: the caller waits for the run to finish and gets 200 with {"execution": "<id>", "state": "end"} (or error, sleep…). Use this mode only for short workflows. When too many such runs are in progress at once, the request gets 429 with Retry-After.

Requests to a workflow that is not published are refused. Request bodies are limited to 1 MB.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
webhookobjectThe request: { method, path, url, query, headers, content_type, body, raw, ip, received_at }
webhook.methodstringThe HTTP method
webhook.pathstringThe path called (/hook/<token>)
webhook.urlstringThe full URL called, with the query string
webhook.queryobjectThe query string parameters, e.g. query.id
webhook.headersobjectLower-case name => value, e.g. headers["user-agent"] (without authorization, cookie and the secret header)
webhook.content_typestringThe content type of the body, without parameters
webhook.bodyanyThe decoded body (JSON or web form), else the body text
webhook.rawstringThe body text as received
webhook.ipstringThe caller address
webhook.received_atstringISO 8601

Example

curl -X POST https://app.example.com/hook/3f9c…e1 \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"order": 1042, "email": "ana@example.com"}'

In the workflow, {{ webhook.body.order }} is 1042 and {{ webhook.body.email }} is the address.

pages.title: Form
pages.summary: Publishes a form page; each submission starts the workflow with the answers.
pages.html:
A Form trigger gives the workflow a page with a form you design. Each time someone sends it, the published workflow runs with the answers. Project members also find the form under Forms in the sidebar.

Settings

SettingDescription
Who can fill it inChoices: Project members (logged in); Anyone with the link. Default: Project members (logged in). Required.
FormRequired.
ButtonDefault: Send.
Message after sendingDefault: Thank you, your answers were sent..
Answers variableThe answers by key; who sent them: <variable>_user. Default: form. Required.

The page's address is shown in the settings, at /form/<token>. It works once the workflow is published.

Designing the form

The Form setting opens the form designer. Add fields: text, e-mail, web address, long text, number, date, date & time, choice, checkbox, switch and hidden values. Titles, paragraphs, dividers and columns lay the form out. For each one, set its label, its key (the name of the answer in the variable), whether it is required, and its rules. A form needs at least one field.

With Who can fill it in set to Anyone with the link, people without a NetFlow9 user can fill it in, for example customers or suppliers. With Project members, they must sign in first.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
formobjectThe answers of the form
form_userobjectWho sent the form (null: someone not logged in)
form_user.idstring
form_user.namestring
form_user.emailstring

For a field with the key amount, the answer is {{ form.amount }}. Who sent the form: {{ form_user.name }}, {{ form_user.email }}. With a public form and a visitor who is not signed in, form_user is empty.

Tip: combine a Form with a Human task for approvals. The form collects the request, and the task asks someone to approve it.

pages.title: File upload
pages.summary: Starts the workflow when a file is uploaded to the project's Files.
pages.html:
The File upload trigger runs the published workflow each time a file is uploaded to the project's Files. You can limit it to some file types, for example only PDF and Excel files.

Settings

SettingDescription
Only these file typesFiles uploaded to this project's Files start the workflow once it is published; none chosen: any file.
File variablee.g. {{ file.id }}, {{ file.filename }}. Default: file. Required.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
fileobjectThe uploaded file: { id, filename, extension, type, size, uploaded_by: { id, name, email } }
file.idstring
file.filenamestring
file.extensionstringLower case, e.g. pdf
file.typestringE.g. PDF, Excel, Image
file.sizenumberBytes
file.uploaded_byobject

Pass {{ file.id }} to the steps that take project files: an AI step's Files, FTP / SFTP Upload, Google Drive or OneDrive upload, email attachments.

pages.title: Email (inbound)
pages.summary: Starts the workflow when an email arrives at the workflow's own address.
pages.html:
The Email (inbound) trigger gives the workflow an email address. Each message sent to it starts the published workflow, with the message, including its attachments, in a variable.

Note: this trigger is available when the installation receives mail (see Inbound mail). Addresses start with your account's email prefix, set under Settings → Inbound mail.

Settings

SettingDescription
AddressMail sent here starts the workflow once it is published (the start is your account's email prefix: Settings, Inbound mail).
Accept mail only fromOne sender address or @domain per line (the envelope sender); empty: anyone.
Save attachments as project filesDefault: on.
Message variablee.g. {{ mail.subject }}, {{ mail.text }}. Default: mail. Required.

Variables

The message variable (default mail) holds:

FieldDescription
mail.from, mail.from_nameThe sender's address and name.
mail.to, mail.cc, mail.reply_toLists of addresses.
mail.subjectThe subject.
mail.text, mail.htmlThe text and HTML bodies.
mail.dateWhen it was sent (ISO 8601).
mail.attachmentsA list of { filename, contentType, size, disposition, file }. file is the id of the saved project file.
mail.attachment_count, mail.attachment_filesThe number of attachments, and their file ids.
mail.message_id, mail.in_reply_to, mail.referencesFor threading replies.
mail.headersAll headers, lower-case names, e.g. {{ mail.headers["x-priority"] }}.
mail.recipientThe address it was sent to.

To read an existing mailbox instead (IMAP, Gmail, Microsoft 365), use a Schedule Trigger followed by Read emails (IMAP).

pages.title: Steps
pages.summary: All the steps you can add after a trigger: logic, data, files, email, people, AI and integrations.
pages.html:
After the trigger, a workflow is made of steps. Each step does one thing and passes its results to the next steps through variables. Here are all of them, by kind.

Logic

StepWhat it does
IfTests conditions: continues on true or false.
SwitchCompares a value with cases: one output per case.
LoopRuns the steps inside it for each item of a list.
MergeJoins branches: continues when all of them arrived, or at the first one.
SetSets a variable.
WaitPauses the run for a while.
CodeRuns a short script (J, a JavaScript subset).
NoteA comment on the canvas. It is not connected and does nothing.
ActionAn empty step that passes the run on: a placeholder while you sketch a workflow.

Data, files and email

StepWhat it does
HTTP RequestCalls any web API.
Data TableReads and writes the project's data tables.
Download FileSaves a file from a URL in the project's Files.
FTP / SFTPDownloads or lists files on a server.
FTP / SFTP UploadSends files to a server.
Send emailSends a designed email.
Read emails (IMAP)Reads messages from a mailbox.

People

StepWhat it does
Human taskAsks someone to complete a form, and waits.

AI and integrations

  • AI steps: Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI, Gemini (Google), Ollama, Lemonade AI.
  • Google: Gmail, Google Drive, Google Sheets, Google Calendar, Google Docs.
  • Microsoft 365: Outlook Mail, Outlook Calendar, OneDrive / SharePoint, Excel, Microsoft Teams.
  • LDAP: search and manage directory entries.
  • Database: query and change SQL databases.

Some steps depend on what the installation provides, such as Database (the database drivers). Steps that aren't available don't appear in the step list.

What steps have in common

  • A name, shown on the canvas. Give steps names that say what they do: Get open orders rather than HTTP Request.
  • A result variable, for steps that produce something. You can rename it to tell two steps of the same kind apart.
  • On error, for steps that call other systems: fail the step (and the run), or continue on an error output. See Errors, limits and timeouts.
  • Expressions in most fields, to use the data of earlier steps.

pages.title: If
pages.summary: Tests one or more conditions and continues on its true or false output.
pages.html:
The If step tests conditions and continues on its true output when they hold, or on false otherwise.

Settings

SettingDescription
True whenChoices: All conditions hold; Any condition holds. Default: All conditions hold. Required.
ConditionsCompared as numbers when both sides are numbers, else as text; a list "contains" one of its items, "is empty" when it has none. Rows of: Test, Operator, Value.

Each condition compares a Test, an expression such as {{ mail.subject }} or {{ response.status }}, with a Value. The operators: equals, not equal, greater than, greater than or equal to, less than, less than or equal to, contains, starts with, is one of, is empty, is not empty.

How values are compared

  • Two numbers are compared as numbers (10 is greater than 9). Otherwise both sides are compared as text.
  • contains on text looks for a part of it. On a list, it looks for an item.
  • is one of takes a list, or text separated by commas: new, open, pending.
  • is empty is true for a missing value, an empty text (or only spaces), false, and a list with no items.

Example

True when an email is urgent: True when = Any condition holds, with {{ mail.subject }} contains URGENT, and {{ mail.headers["x-priority"] }} equals 1.

pages.title: Switch
pages.summary: Compares one value with several cases; each case has its own output.
pages.html:
Switch takes one value and compares it case by case. The first case that matches continues on its own output. When none matches, the run continues on otherwise. Use it instead of a chain of If steps.

Settings

SettingDescription
VariableRequired.
CasesChecked in order: the first matching case continues on its output, else otherwise. Rows of: Output, Operator, Value. Required.

The Variable is a reference such as {{ ticket.category }}. Each case has an Output name, which is shown on the canvas, an operator and a value. The operators and comparison rules are those of If. A Switch has at most 20 cases.

Example

OutputOperatorValue
billingis one ofinvoice, payment, refund
supportequalssupport
salesstarts withsales

The step then has four outputs: billing, support, sales and otherwise.

pages.title: Loop
pages.summary: Runs the steps inside it once for each item of a list.
pages.html:
A Loop is a box on the canvas that holds other steps. It runs them once for each item of a list: the emails read, the rows of a table, the files downloaded. After the last item, the run continues on the loop's output.

Settings

SettingDescription
ListOne expression giving a list, at most 1000 items. Required.
Item variableThe current item, inside the loop. Default: item. Required.
Position variableThe current item's position (0, 1, ...). Default: index. Required.
CollectOptional: evaluated at the end of each pass, the values listed in the result's results, e.g. {{ ai.json }}.
Result variableAfter the loop: { count, results, errors }. Default: loop. Required.
On error in a passChoices: Stop the workflow; Skip the item and continue. Default: Stop the workflow. Required.

How it runs

  • The steps inside start at the inner step that has no incoming connection.
  • In each pass, the current item is in item and its position (0, 1, …) in index. You can rename both.
  • A pass ends when nothing is left running inside the loop. Then the next item starts.
  • A loop takes at most 1000 items.
  • Collect keeps one value per pass, such as each item's AI answer. They are listed in loop.results.
  • With Skip the item and continue, a failing step ends only that pass. The error is listed in loop.errors, and the loop goes on.
  • Wait steps and human tasks work inside a loop: the run sleeps and continues with the same item later.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
loopobjectThe loop's result: { count, results, errors }
loop.countnumberThe passes
loop.resultsarrayThe Collect values, one per pass (none when Collect is empty)
loop.errorsarraySkipped items

The item and position variables exist only inside the loop.

Example

After Read emails (variable mails): a Loop over {{ mails }}. Inside it, a Data Table step that inserts {{ item.from }} and {{ item.subject }}.

pages.title: Merge
pages.summary: Joins branches: continues once all of them arrived, or at the first one.
pages.html:
Merge joins branches back into one path. It has two inputs and one output. Its setting decides when it continues:

Settings

SettingDescription
Continue whenAll: waits for every branch that can still arrive; first: goes on at once, the later ones end there. Choices: All incoming branches arrived; The first branch arrived (the others are ignored). Default: All incoming branches arrived. Required.

All incoming branches arrived (default)

Merge waits until a run has arrived on every incoming connection, then continues once. Use it after branches that run side by side, for example two HTTP requests whose results the next step needs together.

When only some branches can arrive, as after an If, where only true or false runs, Merge continues as soon as nothing else can reach it. So it also brings the two sides of an If back together.

The first branch arrived

Merge continues as soon as the first branch arrives. Branches that arrive later end at the Merge: nothing continues for them, so the steps after the Merge run only once. Use it when any one result is enough, such as the first of two sources that answers, or a reminder path racing a Wait.

The other branches are not stopped: their steps still run until they reach the Merge. Inside a Loop, each pass starts again: the first branch of every pass continues.

Merge sets no variables. The variables set on each branch stay available after it, including those of branches that arrived after a first branch Merge continued.

pages.title: Set
pages.summary: Sets a variable to a value, for the steps after it.
pages.html:
Set stores a value in a variable. Use it to compute a value once and reuse it, to give a long expression a short name, or to keep a counter.

Settings

SettingDescription
VariableLetters, digits or underscore. Required.
ValueText.

The value may be text with expressions (INV-{{ order.number }}), or one expression alone. An expression alone keeps its type: {{ response.body.items }} stores the list itself, not its text.

A variable can't be named vars: that name is taken by the project variables.

pages.title: Wait
pages.summary: Pauses the run for a while, then continues.
pages.html:
Wait pauses the run for the time you set, then continues on its output. Meanwhile the execution is in the Sleep state and uses no resources. It is woken up when the time comes.

Settings

SettingDescription
Wait forDefault: 1. Required.
UnitsChoices: Seconds; Minutes; Hours; Days. Default: Minutes. Required.

Use it for reminders (wait 2 days, then send a reminder if the task is still open), to space out calls to an API with rate limits, or to give another system time to process something before you check the result.

pages.title: Code
pages.summary: Runs a short script (a safe subset of JavaScript) that reads and sets workflow variables.
pages.html:
Code runs a short script written in J, a safe subset of JavaScript. Use it for what is awkward to do with other steps: reshaping data, calculations, text processing.

Settings

SettingDescription
CodeJ (JavaScript subset): workflow variables are plain names, assigning one sets it (total = items.length); let / const stay local; vars.<name> = project variables; console.log() writes to the log. Required.
Timeout (seconds)Default: 5. Required.
On errorAn error in the code, or a limit reached. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Writing code

  • Workflow variables are plain names: mails.length, response.body.total.
  • Assigning to a name sets a workflow variable for the next steps, even a new one: total = items.length.
  • let, const and functions stay local to the script.
  • Project variables are read-only: vars.base_url.
  • console.log(...) writes to the execution log (the first 50 lines).
// totals per customer from a list of orders
let byCustomer = {};
for (const o of orders) {
  byCustomer[o.customer] = (byCustomer[o.customer] ?? 0) + o.amount;
}
totals = Object.entries(byCustomer).map((e) => ({ name: e[0], sum: e[1] }));
console.log("customers:", totals.length);

J supports most of everyday JavaScript, but not classes, new, async or destructuring. See The expression language.

Limits

A script stops when it reaches its timeout (at most 30 seconds) or a limit on the number of operations. Its code is limited to 100,000 characters. With Continue on the error output, the message is in the error variable.

pages.title: HTTP Request
pages.summary: Calls any web API: method, URL, query, headers, body, and a credential for authentication.
pages.html:
HTTP Request calls a web API or page and stores the response. Most services without a dedicated step can be reached with it.

Settings

SettingDescription
Response variableDefault: response. Required.
On errorNo answer, timeout, status 400+. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.
MethodChoices: GET; POST; PUT; PATCH; DELETE; HEAD. Default: GET. Required.
URLhttp:// or https://. Required.
Timeout (s)Default: 30. Required.
Query parametersRows of: Name, Value. A name in several rows is sent once per row (columns=a&columns=b).
HeadersRows of: Name, Value.
CredentialAPI key, Basic, Bearer or OAuth credential of the project (menu: Credentials).
BodyChoices: None; JSON; Form (urlencoded); Text. Default: None. Required.
JSON-RPC 2.0Default: off. (Shown for some values of Body.)
ContentJSON: a JSON text, or {{ ... }} giving an object / list. (Shown for some values of Body.)
Form fieldsRows of: Name, Value. (Shown for some values of Body.)

Authentication

Choose a credential of the project instead of typing a key into a header. API key, Basic, Bearer and OAuth credentials add what the service expects to each request, and the secret never shows in the workflow. See Credentials & variables.

The body

  • JSON: write the JSON, with expressions where needed, or use one expression that gives an object or list: {{ order }}. The designer checks that the JSON is valid.
  • JSON-RPC 2.0: wraps the content as a JSON-RPC request.
  • Form (urlencoded): name / value rows.
  • Text: sent as it is.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
responseobjectThe HTTP response: { ok, status, headers, body, error, time_ms }
response.okboolean
response.statusnumber
response.headersobjectLower-case name => value (a list when repeated)
response.bodyanyJSON decoded, else text
response.errorstring
response.time_msnumber

A status of 400 or above counts as an error. By default the step fails. With Continue on the error output, the run takes the error output, and response.status and response.error tell what happened.

Note: by default an HTTP Request may only call public addresses. Calls to the NetFlow9 server itself or its private network are refused unless the installation allows them (see Configuration).

pages.title: Data Table
pages.summary: Queries, inserts, updates and deletes rows of a project data table.
pages.html:
The Data Table step works with the project's data tables: simple tables inside NetFlow9 that workflows share. Choose the table and the operation.

Settings

SettingDescription
TableA data table of the project. Required.
OperationChoices: Query rows; Get a row (by id); Insert a row; Insert rows (a list); Insert or update (by a column); Update a row (by id); Update rows (filter); Delete a row (by id); Delete rows (filter); Get the columns. Default: Query rows. Required.
Row id{{ ... }} for expressions, e.g. {{ table.row.id }}. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
Rows matchingChoices: All conditions; Any condition. Default: All conditions. Required. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
ConditionsNone: every row. Rows of: Column, Operator, Value. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
Sort byA column; empty: in the order added. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
DirectionChoices: Ascending; Descending. Default: Ascending. Required. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
LimitDefault: 100. Required. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
SkipDefault: 0. Required. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
ValuesRows of: Column, Value. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
Match by columnSame value in this column: updated, else inserted. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
RowsAn expression giving a list of objects keyed by column, e.g. {{ response.body.items }}. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
Result variableDefault: table. Required.
On errorA missing row, a column rule, an unknown column. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Operations

  • Query rows: the rows matching the conditions (none: every row), sorted, with Limit and Skip for paging.
  • Insert a row / Update a row: column / value rows. The values may be expressions.
  • Insert rows (a list): one expression giving a list of objects keyed by column, e.g. {{ response.body.items }}.
  • Insert or update: updates the row whose Match by column has the same value, else inserts one. Use it to keep a table in step with another system.
  • Update rows / Delete rows (filter): every row matching the conditions.
  • Get the columns: the table's columns.

Values are checked against the column types and rules. A value that doesn't fit is an error.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
tableobjectThe Data Table result: { rows, count, total }
table.rowsarray
table.countnumber
table.totalnumber
table.errorstringOn error only

Besides id, created_at and updated_at, each row has its columns by name: {{ table.rows[0].email }}.

pages.title: Download File
pages.summary: Downloads a file from a URL into the project's Files.
pages.html:
Download File fetches a file from an address and saves it in the project's Files. The next steps can use it: attach it to an email, give it to an AI step, upload it elsewhere.

Settings

SettingDescription
URLThe file (GET): http(s):// or a data: URL. Required.
CredentialAPI key, Basic, Bearer or OAuth credential of the project (menu: Credentials).
Query parametersRows of: Name, Value. A name in several rows is sent once per row (columns=a&columns=b).
HeadersRows of: Name, Value.
File nameEmpty: the name the server gives, else the last part of the URL.
Largest size (MB)Default: 25. Required.
Timeout (s)Default: 120. Required.
File variableDefault: file. Required.
On errorNo answer, timeout, status 400+, too large. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
fileobjectThe saved file: { id, filename, size, contentType, isImage, width, height, imageType }
file.idstring
file.filenamestring
file.sizenumberBytes
file.contentTypestring
file.isImagebooleanAn image, by its content
file.widthnumberPixels (images; null for SVG)
file.heightnumberPixels (images; null for SVG)
file.imageTypestringThe real image type, e.g. image/png

pages.title: FTP / SFTP
pages.summary: Downloads or lists files on an FTP, FTPS or SFTP server, with filters, decryption and signature checks.
pages.html:
FTP / SFTP downloads files from a server into the project's Files, or only lists them. It is built for file exchanges with partners: it can pick only the new files, leave files still being written, decrypt PGP / S/MIME files and check signatures, then delete or move the files it took.

Settings

SettingDescription
Server credentialAn FTP / SFTP server credential of the project (menu: Credentials). Required.
ActionChoices: Download files; List files (no download). Default: Download files. Required.
Folder/out/reports (from the root) or out/reports; empty: the start folder.
File names*.csv, report_????.xlsx, 2026/*.csv or /^inv_\d+\.xml$/i; any case. Default: *.
Leave outNames not taken (e.g. files still being uploaded). Default: *.part, *.tmp, *.filepart, .*.
Include subfoldersDefault: off.
Levels of subfoldersDefault: 3. (Shown for some values of Include subfolders.)
Modified after2026-10-01, -24 hours, yesterday; empty: any.
Modified beforeAs Modified after; empty: any.
Unchanged for at least (minutes)Leaves files changed in the last minutes. Default: 0.
Only new filesNot taken by an earlier run (or changed). Default: off.
OrderChoices: Oldest first; Newest first; By name. Default: Oldest first. Required.
Smallest size (KB)Smaller files are left; 0: also empty files. Default: 0.
Largest size (MB)Larger files are left (in skipped). Default: 25. Required.
Files per runThe rest wait for the next run. Default: 20. Required.
DecryptThe ending is removed: report.csv.gpg -> report.csv. Choices: No; Files with an encrypted ending (.gpg, .pgp, .asc, .enc, .p7m, ...); All files. Default: No. Required. (Shown for some values of Action.)
Decryption keyA Decryption key credential: PGP / GPG, OpenSSL or S/MIME. (Shown for some values of Decrypt.)
Decompress .gz / .bz2 filesAfter decrypting: report.csv.gz -> report.csv. Default: off. (Shown for some values of Action.)
Check signatureBad, or by another key: not saved. Choices: No; In the file (PGP signed, S/MIME .p7m); A separate signature file next to it (.sig, .asc, .p7s). Default: No. Required. (Shown for some values of Action.)
Verification keyA Verification key credential: the sender's key or certificate. (Shown for some values of Check signature.)
No signature fileChoices: Leave the file for the next run (its signature may still be coming); An error. Default: Leave the file for the next run (its signature may still be coming). Required. (Shown for some values of Check signature.)
AfterwardsOnly for the files saved. Choices: Leave them on the server; Delete them from the server; Move them to a folder on the server. Default: Leave them on the server. Required. (Shown for some values of Action.)
Move to folderMade when missing. (Shown for some values of Afterwards.)
Timeout per file (s)Default: 120. Required.
Result variablee.g. a Loop over {{ ftp.files }}. Default: ftp. Required.
On errorNo connection, unreadable folder, failed file. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
ftpobjectThe files downloaded: { files, count, skipped, errors, error }
ftp.filesarray
ftp.countnumber
ftp.skippedarrayFiles matching but left: too large, a type that cannot be saved
ftp.errorsarray
ftp.errorstringThe first error, or null

Follow it with a Loop over {{ ftp.files }}, and pass {{ item.id }} to the steps that read files.

pages.title: FTP / SFTP Upload
pages.summary: Sends project files or a text to an FTP, FTPS or SFTP server, optionally compressed, encrypted and signed.
pages.html:
FTP / SFTP Upload sends project files, or a text you write (CSV, XML…), to a server. Files are sent as .part and renamed when complete, so the receiver never sees half a file. They can be compressed, encrypted for the receiver, and signed.

Settings

SettingDescription
Server credentialAn FTP / SFTP server credential of the project (menu: Credentials). Required.
SendChoices: Project files; A text (CSV, XML, ...). Default: Project files. Required.
A file with that name is thereChoices: Replace it; Leave it, do not send; Add a number to the name (report_1.csv); An error. Default: Replace it. Required.
Folder/in/orders (from the root) or in/orders; empty: the start folder.
Name on the serverEmpty: the file's name; {name} {base} {ext} {date} {time} {n}.
Project filesFile ids separated by commas, or {{ ... }}, e.g. {{ file.id }}, {{ ftp.files }}. (Shown for some values of Send.)
ContentThe file's text. (Shown for some values of Send.)
Make missing foldersDefault: on.
Send as .part, rename when completeNo half files seen; off: servers refusing renames. Default: on.
Compress (gzip, .gz)Default: off.
Check the size on the serverDefault: on.
EncryptAfter compressing (.gpg, .asc, .enc, .p7m). Default: off.
Encryption keyAn Encryption key credential: the recipient's PGP key, a passphrase, an OpenSSL password or S/MIME certificate. (Shown for some values of Encrypt.)
SignWith your private key: the receiver can check it. Default: off.
Signing keyA Signing key credential: PGP, S/MIME certificate + key, or a private key. (Shown for some values of Sign.)
SignatureA plain private key: always a separate file. Choices: In the file (signed, then encrypted); A separate signature file next to it (.sig, .asc, .p7s). Default: In the file (signed, then encrypted). Required. (Shown for some values of Sign.)
Timeout per file (s)Default: 120. Required.
Result variablee.g. {{ upload.count }}. Default: upload. Required.
On errorNo connection, or a failed file. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

In Name on the server, {name} is the file's name, {base} and {ext} its parts, {date} and {time} the current date and time, and {n} a counter. Example: orders_{date}_{n}.csv.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
uploadobjectThe files sent: { files, count, skipped, errors, error }
upload.filesarray
upload.countnumber
upload.skippedarrayFiles not sent: one of that name is there
upload.errorsarray
upload.errorstringThe first error, or null

pages.title: Send email
pages.summary: Sends an email designed with blocks of rich text and images, with expressions.
pages.html:
Send email sends a message from the installation's sending address. You design the message in an email designer, and it is sent as responsive HTML with a text version.

Settings

SettingDescription
ToAddresses separated by commas, or an expression giving one or a list, e.g. {{ form.email }}. Required.
Cc 
Bcc 
SubjectRequired.
Sender nameSent from noreply@netflow9.io. Default: NetFlow9.
Reply toWhere replies go (empty: nowhere useful).
MessageRequired.

The message

The Message is made of blocks, one under the other:

  • Text: rich text with headings, lists, links, bold and italic. It may hold expressions: Hello {{ form_user.name }}.
  • Image: an image from the project's Files, embedded in the email, with its width, alignment and an optional link.

The preheader is the short text that mail apps show next to the subject. An email holds at most 50 blocks, and images are PNG, JPEG or GIF (the types every mail app shows).

To include an AI answer formatted, use {{ ai.html }} in a text block.

Tip: to send from your own mailbox instead, so replies come back to you, use Gmail or Outlook Mail.

pages.title: Read emails (IMAP)
pages.summary: Reads messages from a mailbox folder (IMAP, Google Mail, Microsoft 365) into a list.
pages.html:
Read emails reads messages from a folder of a mailbox and puts them in a list variable, oldest first. It works with any IMAP server, and with Google Mail and Microsoft 365 credentials. Usually it follows a Schedule Trigger, with a Loop after it to handle each message.

Settings

SettingDescription
Mail credentialIMAP, Google Mail or Microsoft 365 Mail credential of the project. Required.
FolderDefault: INBOX. Required.
Messages variablee.g. a Loop over {{ mails }}. Default: mails. Required.
ReadNew: the first run notes where the folder ends; the next runs read what arrives. Choices: New messages (arrived since the last run); Unread messages; All messages in the folder. Default: New messages (arrived since the last run). Required.
AfterwardsChoices: Leave them as they are; Mark them as read; Move them to another folder; Delete them. Default: Leave them as they are. Required.
Move to folder(Shown for some values of Afterwards.)
Save attachments as project filesDefault: on.
Messages per runOldest first; the rest wait for the next run. Default: 10. Required.
Largest message (MB)Larger messages are skipped. Default: 25. Required.

New messages

With New messages, the first run only notes where the folder ends and reads nothing. Each later run reads what arrived since the previous one. This mode needs no change to the mailbox, so you can leave the messages as they are.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
mailsarrayThe messages read (oldest first; empty when there are none): [ { subject, from, text, html, attachments, ... } ]
mails[i].accountstringThe mail credential
mails[i].folderstring
mails[i].uidnumber
mails[i].message_idstring
mails[i].fromstringThe sender address
mails[i].from_namestringThe sender name
mails[i].toarray
mails[i].ccarray
mails[i].reply_toarray
mails[i].subjectstring
mails[i].datestringISO 8601
mails[i].textstringThe text body
mails[i].htmlstringThe HTML body
mails[i].in_reply_tostring
mails[i].referencesarray
mails[i].headersobjectLower-case name => value (a list when repeated), e.g. headers["x-mailer"]
mails[i].attachmentsarray
mails[i].attachment_countnumber
mails[i].attachment_filesarrayThe saved file ids

pages.title: Human task
pages.summary: Asks a person to complete a form, and waits for the answer.
pages.html:
A Human task puts a task in the My tasks list of the people it is assigned to. The run sleeps until one of them completes the task's form, then continues with the answers. Use it for approvals, reviews and anything a person must decide.

Settings

SettingDescription
TaskIts name in My tasks; {{ }} for expressions, e.g. Approve {{ form.amount }} EUR. Default: Please complete this task. Required.
InstructionsShown above the form; {{ }} for expressions.
Assigned users 
Assigned rolesNo user and no role: any project member.
Also assigned toOptional: an expression giving a user (id, username or e-mail), e.g. {{ form_user.id }}.
FormRequired.
ButtonDefault: Complete.
Time limitChoices: No time limit; Minutes; Hours; Days. Default: No time limit. Required.
AfterDefault: 1. (Shown for some values of Time limit.)
Answers variableThe answers by key; who gave them: <variable>_user. Default: task. Required.

Assignment

Assign the task to users, to roles, or both. Anyone who matches can complete it. Also assigned to adds a user from the run, e.g. the manager found earlier: {{ manager.email }}. With no user and no role, any member of the project can complete it.

Time limit

With a time limit, the step has two outputs: done when someone completed the task in time, and timeout when the time passed first. The task then expires. Use the timeout output to remind someone, escalate, or decide automatically.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
taskobjectThe answers of the task
task_userobjectWho completed the task
task_user.idstring
task_user.namestring
task_user.emailstring

The answers are keyed by the form's field keys: a field decision gives {{ task.decision }}.

Example: an approval

  1. A Form collects an expense: amount, reason.
  2. A Human task Approve {{ form.amount }} EUR for {{ form_user.name }}, assigned to the Managers role, with a field decision (Choice: approve / reject) and a field comment.
  3. An If on {{ task.decision }} equals approve sends the approval or the rejection by email.

pages.title: AI steps
pages.summary: Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama and Lemonade: prompts, JSON answers, files (images, PDF, text, Office), and tools the model may use.
pages.html:
The AI steps send a prompt to a language model and store its answer. They all work the same way. Only the provider, and a few settings of its own, differ:

StepProviderOwn settings
Claude (Anthropic)Anthropic's APIEffort (low … max), Fallback on refusal
OpenAIOpenAI's API, or a compatible serverTemperature
Gemini (Google)Google's Gemini APIThinking, Temperature
OllamaAn Ollama server you runTemperature, Thinking, Context length, Keep the model loaded
Lemonade AIA Lemonade server you runTemperature

Credential: your own key, or the System AI

Each step needs a credential of its provider, created under Credentials with your API key or your server's address. If the installation offers a System AI of the same provider, it is listed first. It needs no key of your own, and its use is paid with your account's AI credits. Each call counts its tokens in credits, a run stops before a call once its credits are used up, and the account's usage page shows what was spent.

Common settings

SettingDescription
CredentialAnthropic credential. Required.
ModelOr type a name. Default: claude-opus-5-5. Required.
System promptWho the model is and how it works (optional).
PromptThe request; {{ ... }} for expressions, e.g. {{ mail.text }}. Required.
AnswerJSON: parsed (variable .json). Choices: Text; JSON. Default: Text. Required.
FilesOptional: images, PDF, text or Office files (at most 20): {{ file.id }}, a list, or file ids.
PDFs asAuto: documents if the model reads them. Choices: Auto; Documents; Text and images. Default: Auto. Required.
Result variableDefault: ai. Required.
JSON schemaOptional: the JSON schema the answer must follow, e.g. {"type": "object", "properties": {"category": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["category"], "additionalProperties": false}. (Shown for some values of Answer.)
RoundsCalls to the model (tool uses too). Default: 10. Required.
Max tokensLongest answer per call. Default: 16000. Required.
Timeout (s)Per call to the model. Default: 300. Required.
On errorUnreachable, declined, cut off, bad JSON. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Text or JSON answers

With Answer = Text, the answer is in ai.text, and in ai.html as safe HTML converted from the model's Markdown. Use {{ ai.html }} in a Send email text block to keep the formatting.

With Answer = JSON, the answer is parsed into ai.json, so the next steps can use its fields: {{ ai.json.category }}. Add a JSON schema to require a shape, for example:

{"type": "object",
 "properties": {
   "category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "support", "sales"]},
   "urgent":   {"type": "boolean"}
 },
 "required": ["category", "urgent"],
 "additionalProperties": false}

An answer that is not valid JSON is an error. Choose On error to fail, or to continue on the error output.

Files

Give the model files from the project's Files with the prompt, such as a scanned invoice, a contract or a report: {{ file.id }}, a list of ids (for example {{ mail.attachment_files }}), or ids separated by commas. Up to 20 files per prompt:

  • Images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP; 5 MB each): the model looks at them.
  • PDF (20 MB each): sent as set by PDFs as, below.
  • Office documents (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument: docx, xlsx, pptx, odt, ods, odp): their text. A spreadsheet is sent sheet by sheet, as CSV rows.
  • Text files (txt, csv, tsv, md, json, xml, yaml, html, log): as they are, in UTF-8.

The text of a file is cut after 200,000 characters, and a prompt sends at most 30 MB of files. Other file types, such as zip archives, are refused.

PDFs as

ChoiceWhat the model gets
AutoThe PDF itself where the model reads PDFs: Claude, Gemini, and the OpenAI step on OpenAI's own API. Elsewhere (Lemonade, Ollama, other OpenAI-compatible servers) its text and images.
DocumentsThe PDF itself: the model reads its layout, tables and scanned pages. Not offered by the Ollama step.
Text and imagesThe text of its pages and up to 10 of its images: fewer tokens, for any model. A scanned PDF (without text) or an encrypted one cannot be read this way: send it as a document.

Note: Steps saved before Files existed keep their Images: they are moved to Files the next time the workflow is saved.

Tools

The model can do more than answer. It can use tools during the step, and the step goes back and forth with the model until the model has a final answer or Rounds is reached.

  • Use these tools: what the model may do in this project: list and query data tables, insert, update or delete rows, change tables and columns, list and run workflows, read executions, list and read files (text, PDF and Office documents), look at images, and read the project variables. Choose only what the task needs. Reading is on by default, writing is off.
  • MCP servers: the tools of external MCP servers, added as MCP credentials of the project.
  • Tool servers: tools that the installation runs for your account, such as a web browser the model can use to open pages.

Each tool call is listed in ai.tool_calls.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
aiobjectThe answer: { text, html, json, model, stop_reason, rounds, tool_calls, usage }; on error { error }
ai.textstringThe answer
ai.htmlstringThe answer as safe HTML (its Markdown converted); in an email {{ ai.html }} shows it formatted
ai.jsonanyThe answer as JSON (answer: JSON)
ai.modelstring
ai.stop_reasonstring
ai.roundsnumber
ai.tool_callsarray
ai.usageobject
ai.errorstringOn error only

Claude: effort and fallback

Effort sets how much the model thinks before answering: higher for harder tasks, lower for speed and cost. When a request is declined, Fallback on refusal (on by default) lets Anthropic retry it on the model they recommend, for models that support it.

Example: classify incoming mail

  1. Email (inbound) trigger, variable mail.
  2. Claude: system prompt "You sort customer emails.", prompt Subject: {{ mail.subject }} and {{ mail.text }}, Answer: JSON, with the schema above.
  3. Switch on {{ ai.json.category }}: one branch per team, each forwarding the mail.

pages.title: Integrations
pages.summary: Steps for Google, Microsoft 365, LDAP directories and SQL databases.
pages.html:
Besides the general steps, NetFlow9 has steps for these services:

  • Google: Gmail, Google Drive, Google Sheets, Google Calendar, Google Docs.
  • Microsoft 365: Outlook Mail, Outlook Calendar, OneDrive / SharePoint, Excel, Microsoft Teams.
  • LDAP: directory entries, groups and passwords.
  • Database: SQL databases (MySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Firebird, ODBC).

For any other service with a web API, use HTTP Request with an API key or OAuth credential. For services with an MCP server, an AI step can use its tools.

pages.title: Google
pages.summary: Gmail, Google Drive, Google Sheets, Google Calendar and Google Docs steps.
pages.html:
The Google steps work with a Google account through OAuth credentials. Create the credential under Credentials and connect it to the Google account. Setting up the OAuth app, below, explains how to register it and get its client ID and secret. The steps act with that account's rights. They are part of NetFlow9 itself, on every plan, Free included.

StepCredentialOperations
GmailGoogle Mail (OAuth)Send a message; create a draft; search / read messages; get a message; mark / archive / label a message; move a message to the trash; list the labels
Google DriveGoogle Drive (OAuth)List / search files; get file information; download a file (into the project Files); upload a file; create a folder; move a file; share a file; delete a file
Google SheetsGoogle Sheets or Google Drive (OAuth)Read rows; append rows; update cells; clear cells; get spreadsheet information; create a spreadsheet; add a sheet
Google CalendarGoogle Calendar (OAuth)List events; get an event; create an event; update an event; delete an event; quick add (from a sentence); find busy times; list the calendars
Google DocsGoogle Docs or Google Drive (OAuth)Read a document; create a document; append content; replace texts (fill a template); copy a document (a template)

Useful details

  • Gmail search uses Gmail's own syntax: from:ana@example.com has:attachment newer_than:2d. Attachments can be saved as project files.
  • Gmail send sends from the connected mailbox, so replies come back to it. In reply to keeps a message in its thread.
  • Drive download exports Google files: Docs, Sheets and Slides as Office files, PDF, CSV and more.
  • Sheets read can treat the first row as the header. Each row then becomes an object: {{ sheet.rows[0].Email }}.
  • Docs templates: copy a template document, then Replace texts with an object of placeholders. Each {{key}} in the document gets its value.
  • Calendar create can add a Google Meet link and invite guests.

Every step has On error, a timeout and a result variable. The designer suggests the result's fields as you type.

Setting up the OAuth app

The credentials connect through your own OAuth app at Google: you register it once, then paste its client ID and client secret into the credentials. One app can serve all your Google credentials.

What each credential needs

CredentialEnable this APIScope requestedUsed by
Google Mail (OAuth)Gmail APIhttps://mail.google.com/Gmail step, Read emails (IMAP)
Google Drive (OAuth)Google Drive API (+ Sheets / Docs API for those steps)https://www.googleapis.com/auth/driveGoogle Drive step; also Sheets and Docs steps; HTTP Request
Google Sheets (OAuth)Google Sheets APIhttps://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheetsGoogle Sheets step; HTTP Request
Google Calendar (OAuth)Google Calendar APIhttps://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendarGoogle Calendar step; HTTP Request
Google Docs (OAuth)Google Docs API (+ Drive API to copy templates)https://www.googleapis.com/auth/documentsGoogle Docs step; HTTP Request

Every credential also asks for openid and email, to show which Google account it is connected to. It asks for offline access, so NetFlow9 can renew its access by itself.

1. Create a Google Cloud project

  1. Open the Google Cloud Console and sign in with the Google account that will own the app, ideally an administrator of your Google Workspace.
  2. In the project picker at the top, click New project, name it (e.g. NetFlow9) and create it. Make sure it is selected.

2. Enable the APIs

  1. Go to APIs & Services → Library.
  2. Search for each API you need (table above), such as Gmail API or Google Drive API, open it and click Enable.

Note: a credential that connects but fails in its step with a message like "API has not been used in project … or it is disabled" is missing its API. Enable it and try again after a minute.

3. Configure the consent screen

Go to Google Auth Platform (called OAuth consent screen in older consoles).

  1. Branding: the app name people see when they connect (e.g. NetFlow9), a support email, and optionally your logo and domain.
  2. Audience:
    • Internal: only users of your Google Workspace organization can connect. No verification by Google is needed. This is the simplest choice for a company.
    • External: any Google account. While the app is in Testing, only the test users you add here can connect, and their connections expire after 7 days. Publish the app (In production) for lasting connections. Google may then require verification, because Gmail and Drive scopes are sensitive or restricted.
  3. Data access: click Add or remove scopes and add the scopes of the credentials you will use (table above).

4. Create the OAuth client

  1. Go to Clients (or APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID).
  2. Application type: Web application. Give it a name.
  3. Under Authorized redirect URIs, click Add URI and paste NetFlow9's redirect URI. It is shown in every OAuth credential's form, and has the form: 
    https://<your NetFlow9 address>/credential/oauth_callback
    It must match exactly: https, the host, and no trailing slash.
  4. Click Create.

5. Copy the client ID and secret

Google shows the Client ID (ending in .apps.googleusercontent.com) and the Client secret. Copy both, or download the JSON file.

Warning: new Google consoles show the client secret only when it is created. If you lose it, open the client, add a new secret, update the credentials in NetFlow9, then delete the old secret. Treat the secret like a password.

To find the client again later: Google Auth Platform → Clients (or APIs & Services → Credentials), then click its name. The Client ID is always shown there.

6. Create and connect the credential in NetFlow9

  1. In the project, open Credentials & variables and add a credential of the kind you need, such as Google Drive (OAuth).
  2. Paste the Client ID and Client secret, then save.
  3. Click Connect. Google asks you to sign in and to allow the access. You come back to NetFlow9, and Account shows the connected address.
  4. Click Test to check it.

The credential acts as the Google account that connected it: workflows see what that account sees. Connect with a dedicated account (e.g. automation@yourcompany.com) rather than a person's when workflows are shared.

Troubleshooting

MessageFix
redirect_uri_mismatchThe redirect URI in the Google client doesn't match NetFlow9's exactly. Copy it again from the credential's form.
access_denied, app not verified, blockedExternal app in Testing: add the account as a test user. Or use an Internal app.
The connection stops working after a weekExternal app in Testing: publish it to production.
API has not been used in project… or it is disabledEnable that API (step 2).
invalid_clientWrong client ID or secret, or the secret was deleted. Paste the current ones.
Insufficient permission / scopeThe scope wasn't granted: add it under Data access, then click Connect again.

pages.title: Microsoft 365
pages.summary: Outlook Mail, Outlook Calendar, OneDrive / SharePoint, Excel and Microsoft Teams steps.
pages.html:
The Microsoft 365 steps use Microsoft Graph through OAuth credentials. Create the credential under Credentials and connect it to a Microsoft account (work, school or personal). Setting up the Entra app, below, explains how to register it and get its client ID and secret. The steps are part of NetFlow9 itself, on every plan, Free included.

StepCredentialOperations
Outlook MailOutlook Mail (Microsoft Graph)Send a message; create a draft; search / read messages; get a message; mark / move / categorize a message; delete a message; list the folders
Outlook CalendarOutlook Calendar (Microsoft Graph)List events; get an event; create an event; update an event; delete an event; find busy times; list the calendars
OneDrive / SharePointOneDrive & SharePoint (Microsoft Graph)List / search files; get file information; download a file (into the project Files); upload a file; create a folder; move / rename a file; share a file; delete a file
ExcelOneDrive & SharePoint (Microsoft Graph)Read rows; append rows; update cells; clear cells; get workbook information; add a worksheet
Microsoft TeamsMicrosoft Teams (Microsoft Graph)Send a channel message; reply to a channel message; send a chat message; list my teams; list the channels of a team; list my chats

Useful details

  • Folders in OneDrive / SharePoint can be given by id, by path (/Reports) or by a sharing link.
  • Excel works on workbooks stored in OneDrive or SharePoint. With a header row, each row becomes an object, as with Google Sheets.
  • Outlook Mail folders: inbox, archive, sentitems… or a folder id.
  • To read a Microsoft 365 mailbox over IMAP instead, use a Microsoft 365 Mail (OAuth) credential with Read emails (IMAP).

Setting up the Entra app

The credentials connect through your own app registration in Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD). You register it once, then paste its client ID and client secret into the credentials. One app can serve all your Microsoft credentials.

What each credential needs

All are delegated permissions: the credential acts as the person who connects it.

CredentialAPIDelegated permissionsUsed by
Outlook Mail (Microsoft Graph)Microsoft GraphUser.Read, Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.SendOutlook Mail step; HTTP Request
Outlook Calendar (Microsoft Graph)Microsoft GraphUser.Read, Calendars.ReadWrite, Calendars.Read.SharedOutlook Calendar step; HTTP Request
OneDrive & SharePoint (Microsoft Graph)Microsoft GraphUser.Read, Files.ReadWrite.All, Sites.ReadWrite.AllOneDrive / SharePoint and Excel steps; HTTP Request
Microsoft Teams (Microsoft Graph)Microsoft GraphUser.Read, Team.ReadBasic.All, Channel.ReadBasic.All, ChannelMessage.Send, ChatMessage.Send, Chat.ReadBasicTeams step; HTTP Request
Microsoft 365 Mail (OAuth)Office 365 Exchange OnlineIMAP.AccessAsUser.AllRead emails (IMAP)

Every credential also asks for offline_access, openid, email and profile, so NetFlow9 can renew its access and show the connected account. You don't need to add these: Microsoft grants them with sign-in.

1. Register the app

  1. Open the Microsoft Entra admin center and sign in with an account allowed to register apps. In many organizations that means an administrator.
  2. Go to Entra ID → App registrations (or Identity → Applications → App registrations) and click New registration.
  3. Name: what people see when they connect, e.g. NetFlow9.
  4. Supported account types:
    • Accounts in this organizational directory only (single tenant): only your organization. The usual choice.
    • Accounts in any organizational directory (multitenant): work and school accounts of any organization.
    • … and personal Microsoft accounts: also Outlook.com and other personal accounts.
  5. Redirect URI: platform Web, and NetFlow9's redirect URI. It is shown in every OAuth credential's form, and has the form: 
    https://<your NetFlow9 address>/credential/oauth_callback
    It must match exactly: https, the host, and no trailing slash.
  6. Click Register.

2. Copy the client ID (and tenant ID)

The app's Overview page shows:

  • Application (client) ID: the Client ID for NetFlow9.
  • Directory (tenant) ID: needed for a single-tenant app (see step 5).

To find them again later: App registrations → All applications, then click the app.

3. Create the client secret

  1. In the app, go to Certificates & secrets → Client secrets → New client secret.
  2. Give it a description (e.g. NetFlow9) and an expiry. The longest offered is 24 months.
  3. Click Add, then copy the secret's Value at once.

Warning: copy the Value column, not the Secret ID. The value is shown only right after it is created: once you leave the page, it can't be read again. If you lose it, create a new secret.

Note: secrets expire. Note the date. Before it, create a new secret, paste it into your Microsoft credentials (the connections stay), then delete the old one.

4. Add the permissions

  1. In the app, go to API permissions → Add a permission.
  2. For the Graph credentials: choose Microsoft Graph → Delegated permissions, tick the permissions from the table above, and click Add permissions.
  3. For Microsoft 365 Mail (IMAP): Add a permission → APIs my organization uses, search for Office 365 Exchange Online, choose Delegated permissions, tick IMAP.AccessAsUser.All, and add it.
  4. If your organization requires it, or for permissions marked Admin consent required (some Teams and SharePoint permissions), click Grant admin consent for <organization>. An administrator must do this.

5. Create and connect the credential in NetFlow9

  1. In the project, open Credentials & variables and add a credential of the kind you need, such as Outlook Mail (Microsoft Graph).
  2. Paste the Client ID and the secret's value as Client secret.
  3. Set Tenant to match the account types you chose:
    Supported account typesTenant
    This organizational directory onlyThe Directory (tenant) ID, or your domain (e.g. example.com)
    Any organizational directoryorganizations
    Any organizational directory and personal accountscommon (default)
  4. Save, then click Connect. Microsoft asks you to sign in and accept the permissions. You come back to NetFlow9, and Account shows the connected address.
  5. Click Test to check it.

The credential acts as the account that connected it. Connect with a dedicated account (e.g. a shared automation mailbox) rather than a person's when workflows are shared.

Notes

  • Teams works with work and school accounts only.
  • Microsoft 365 Mail (IMAP): IMAP must be allowed for the mailbox in Exchange (Microsoft 365 admin center → the user → Mail → Email apps).
  • Graph credentials also work with HTTP Request, for other Microsoft Graph calls within their permissions.

Troubleshooting

MessageFix
AADSTS50011 (redirect URI mismatch)Add NetFlow9's redirect URI exactly, under the Web platform (Authentication page).
AADSTS7000215 (invalid client secret)You pasted the Secret ID, or the secret expired or was deleted. Paste a current secret's Value.
AADSTS50194 / AADSTS90072 (account not in tenant)The Tenant doesn't match the app's account types, or the account isn't in your organization. Use the tenant ID for single-tenant apps.
AADSTS65001 / Need admin approvalAn administrator must grant consent (API permissions → Grant admin consent).
IMAP: authentication failedCheck IMAP.AccessAsUser.All (Office 365 Exchange Online), and that IMAP is enabled for the mailbox.

pages.title: LDAP
pages.summary: Searches and manages entries of an LDAP directory (Active Directory, OpenLDAP...).
pages.html:
The LDAP step works with a directory such as Active Directory or OpenLDAP, through an LDAP server credential of the project. It acts with the rights of the credential's bind DN. Every account has it, whatever its plan.

Operations

OperationResult
Search entries{ entries, count, truncated }. Each entry has its dn and attributes.
Get an entryThe entry.
Add / modify / rename or move / delete an entry{ dn }
Add / remove a member of a group{ dn }
Check a password{ valid, dn }
Set a password{ dn }
