Use it to provision accounts from an HR form, add people to groups after an approval, or check who someone's manager is before assigning a task.

Note: signing in to NetFlow9 with your directory is a separate feature, which depends on your plan. The step doesn't need it. See LDAP sign-in.

pages.title: Database
pages.summary: Queries and changes SQL databases: MySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Firebird, ODBC.
pages.html:
The Database step reads and changes an SQL database through a database credential of the project: MySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, Firebird, or an ODBC data source. Every account has it. Which kinds you can choose depends on what the installation provides: see What the installation needs below.

Operations

OperationResult
Query rows{ rows, count, columns, truncated }: the rows of a SELECT, each an object keyed by column. At most At most (rows); truncated says there were more.
Execute a statement{ affected, lastInsertId }: an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, a procedure call or a change of the tables. lastInsertId is the new row's id where the database gives one (MySQL, SQL Server), else null.
Insert rows{ affected }: the rows of a list of objects keyed by column, such as {{ response.body.items }}, inserted into Table in one transaction: all of them, or none when one fails.

Each step runs one statement on its own connection. Statements of different steps are not in one transaction.

Values in the SQL

A {{ }} in the SQL is sent to the database as a parameter of the statement, never as SQL text. A value can't change the statement, whatever it holds:

SELECT id, name, email FROM customers
WHERE country = {{ form.country }} AND created_at >= {{ since }}
  • Quotes around a {{ }} are not needed. '{{ name }}' is the same parameter.
  • Build a pattern in the expression: name LIKE {{ '%' + name + '%' }}. A {{ }} inside a quoted text, as in '%{{ name }}%', is an error.
  • Table and column names can't be parameters. Write them in the SQL.
  • Numbers and texts are sent as they are, and an empty value as NULL. True / false are booleans for PostgreSQL, 1 / 0 for the others. Lists and objects are sent as JSON text.

Settings

SettingDescription
DatabaseA database credential of the project (menu: Credentials). Required.
OperationChoices: Query rows; Execute a statement; Insert rows. Default: Query rows. Required.
SQLOne statement. A {{ }} is sent as a parameter: WHERE id = {{ order.id }} (not for table or column names). (Shown for some values of Operation.)
TableA table, or schema.table. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
RowsAn expression giving a list of objects keyed by column, e.g. {{ response.body.items }}. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
At most (rows)More are left out (truncated). Default: 1000. Required. (Shown for some values of Operation.)
Timeout (s)To connect, and of the statement where the database has a limit. Default: 60. Required.
Result variable{ rows, count, ... } or { affected }. Default: db. Required.
On errorDatabase errors, or no connection. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
dbobjectThe Database result
db.rowsarrayQuery rows only
db.countnumberQuery rows only
db.columnsarrayThe column names. Query rows only
db.truncatedbooleanMore rows than At most. Query rows only
db.affectednumberThe rows changed. Execute a statement and Insert rows only
db.lastInsertIdstringThe id of the row inserted, null where the database has none. Execute a statement only
db.errorstringOn error only

Each row has its columns by name: {{ db.rows[0].email }}. Names are as the database gives them: Oracle and Firebird give unquoted names in capitals ({{ db.rows[0].EMAIL }}). Long texts and binary columns are read whole. Binary values are base64 text.

The credentials

Create one under Credentials & variables, in the Database group, and use Test to check that it connects.

CredentialSettings
MySQL / MariaDBServer, port (3306), database (optional), username, password. TLS: none, encrypted, or encrypted with the server's certificate checked.
PostgreSQLServer, port (5432), database, username, password. TLS: none, when the server offers it, encrypted, or encrypted with the certificate and name checked.
Microsoft SQL ServerServer, or a named instance such as sql.example.com\SQLEXPRESS, port (1433), database (optional), username, password, Encrypt the connection, and Trust the server's certificate for a self-signed one.
OracleServer, port (1521), Service name (such as ORCLPDB1), username, password.
FirebirdServer, port (3050), the database's path or alias on the server, username, password.
ODBC data sourceThe name of a data source set up on the NetFlow9 server by its administrator, and a username and password when the data source doesn't hold them.

Note: the step works with the rights of the credential's user. Give that user only what the workflows need, for example read access to the tables they query.

The Timeout applies to connecting. MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQL Server (with Microsoft's driver) also stop a statement that runs longer. For Oracle, Firebird and ODBC, the database's own limits apply.

What the installation needs

Each kind of database needs its PHP extension (a PDO driver). A kind whose extension is missing is not offered for new credentials, and the step isn't in the step list when none is installed.

DatabasePHP extension
MySQL / MariaDBpdo_mysql
PostgreSQLpdo_pgsql
Microsoft SQL Serverpdo_sqlsrv (Microsoft's driver), or pdo_dblib (FreeTDS; encryption as set in freetds.conf)
Oraclepdo_oci, with Oracle's client libraries
Firebirdpdo_firebird
ODBCpdo_odbc, with unixODBC and the database's ODBC driver

Install the extension for both the web server's PHP (PHP-FPM) and the command-line PHP, which runs the daemon. Then restart PHP-FPM and the daemon. The setup wizard's Prerequisites list each kind, and say when the command-line PHP lacks an extension the web one has. A workflow that runs in the daemon without the extension fails with a message naming the missing extension.

ODBC credentials name a data source set up on the server, in odbc.ini. They can't hold a connection string, which could point a driver at files on the NetFlow9 server.

pages.title: Expressions
pages.summary: Using the data of earlier steps in settings: {{ }} expressions, fields, lists, methods and project variables.
pages.html:
Most step settings accept expressions: pieces between {{ and }} that are replaced, when the step runs, by values from the run. The language is a safe subset of JavaScript.

Hello {{ form_user.name }}, your order {{ order.number }} is confirmed.

Text or value

  • A setting that is only one expression (spaces around are fine) gives the value as it is: a number, a list, an object. {{ response.body.items }} is the list itself.
  • A setting with text around expressions gives text. Lists and objects are written as JSON, and an empty value as nothing.

Reaching into data

ExpressionGives
{{ mail.subject }}A field of an object
{{ mail.headers["x-priority"] }}A field whose name has dashes or spaces
{{ mails[0].from }}The first item of a list (positions start at 0)
{{ mails.length }}The number of items
{{ response.body?.data?.id }}Nothing, instead of an error, when a part is missing
{{ vars.support_email }}A project variable

Computing

{{ order.quantity * order.price }}
{{ mail.subject.toUpperCase() }}
{{ mail.from.split("@")[1] }}
{{ response.status === 200 ? "ok" : "failed" }}
{{ form.comment ?? "no comment" }}
{{ table.rows.filter(r => r.status === "open").length }}
{{ table.rows.map(r => r.email).join(", ") }}
{{ Math.round(total * 100) / 100 }}
{{ Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10) }}

Strings, lists and numbers have the usual JavaScript methods: trim, includes, replace, slice, filter, map, find, join, toFixed… plus Math, JSON, Date and regular expressions. Write Date() without new. Dates come out as ISO 8601 text.

Help while typing

In expression fields the designer suggests, after {{, the variables available at that step: those set by the trigger and the steps before it, with their fields and types. It also marks mistakes: an unclosed {{, a syntax error, or a name no earlier step sets.

Where variables come from

  • The trigger: webhook, form, file, mail, schedule_time.
  • Each step's result variable: response, table, ai, task…
  • Set and Code steps, which set variables you name.
  • Inside a loop: item and index.
  • The project variables, always: vars.<name>.

Variables live as long as the run. A later step that sets the same name replaces the value.

Limits

An expression runs in a sandbox: it can only read the run's variables, and it stops if it runs too long (one second). An expression that fails, for example by calling a method on nothing, fails its step, with the reason in the execution's error. Use ?. and ?? for values that may be missing.

The full language reference is in The expression language.

pages.title: Errors, limits and timeouts
pages.summary: What happens when a step fails, how to handle errors in the workflow, and the limits of a run.
pages.html:
When a step fails

By default, a step that fails stops the run. The execution's state becomes Error, with the step's name and the reason, such as HTTP Request: status 503, a timeout, a missing credential, or an expression that failed. The steps after it don't run.

Handling errors in the workflow

Steps that call other systems (HTTP Request, Download File, FTP, Data Table, Code, the AI and integration steps) have an On error setting:

  • Fail the step (default): the run stops, as above.
  • Continue on the error output: the step gets two outputs, success and error. On a failure, the run continues on error, and the result variable tells what went wrong: response.status and response.error, ai.error, table.error, or error for Code.

From the error output you can retry after a Wait, notify someone, log the problem in a data table, or take another way.

In a Loop, On error in a pass = Skip the item and continue keeps one bad item from stopping the others. The skipped items are listed in loop.errors.

Timeouts

StepDefault timeout
HTTP Request30 s
Download File, FTP / SFTP (per file)120 s
Google and Microsoft steps60 s (Google Drive, OneDrive / SharePoint: 120 s)
AI steps (per call to the model)300 s
Code5 s (at most 30)

Limits of a run

  • A run executes at most 10,000 steps, counting each pass of a loop. This protects against endless loops.
  • A loop takes at most 1000 items.
  • An execution keeps the last 500 log lines.
  • An expression may run for one second at most.
  • A webhook request body is at most 1 MB.
  • Runs answered while the caller waits (a webhook set to answer When the workflow ends) are limited per account. Extra requests get 429 and should retry.

Account limits

Your account's plan may limit the number of data tables, the rows in one table, the size of all files, and the System AI credits per month. The Usage page (Settings menu) shows where you stand. A step that would go over a limit fails with a message saying which one.

pages.title: Publishing and versions
pages.summary: Drafts and published versions: publishing, unpublishing, viewing and restoring versions.
pages.html:
A workflow has one draft, the version you edit, and any number of published versions: v1, v2, v3… At most one of them is published at a time, and that is the one the trigger runs.

Publishing

  1. Open the status menu in the toolbar. It says Draft, or v2 published.
  2. Choose Publish the draft as v3, the next number.
  3. Add a note, such as "retry on 503", then confirm.

The draft must have no errors. The new version becomes the published one right away, and the trigger starts using it: the schedule, webhook, form, file upload or email address.

You can also publish and unpublish from the three-dots menu next to a workflow in the sidebar. Published workflows have a green dot.

Working on a published workflow

Editing changes only the draft. The toolbar shows draft changed, and the trigger keeps running the published version until you publish again. So you can work on a live workflow safely, test the draft with Run, and publish when ready.

Unpublishing

Unpublish stops the trigger from starting new runs. Runs already in progress finish. The version is kept: if the draft has not changed, Publish v3 makes it live again.

Versions

Versions, in the status menu, lists every published version with its date, who published it and its note. Open one to see it on the canvas, read-only. From there:

  • Publish again: makes that version the published one, for example to roll back quickly.
  • Copy into the draft: replaces the draft with that version, to continue from it.
  • Duplicate: creates a new workflow from it.
  • Back to the draft: returns to editing.

Duplicating and deleting

Duplicate creates a new workflow from the saved draft, unpublished. Delete removes the workflow with all its versions and executions. This cannot be undone.

pages.title: Executions
pages.summary: Following runs in the designer, reading their log and variables, and the account's execution log.
pages.html:
Each run of a workflow is an execution. It records what started it, the version it ran (or the draft), its state, its log and its variables.

The Executions panel

In the designer, click the clock icon, or press Run, which opens the panel on the new run. The panel lists the workflow's executions, newest first, and refreshes every few seconds. Select one to see:

  • The state, what started it (manual, webhook, schedule…) and the version.
  • The error, if the run failed: the step and the reason.
  • The log: one line per step, with the time, plus the lines your Code steps write with console.log.
  • The variables at the end of the run, or at its current point if it is still running. This is the quickest way to see what each step produced.

States

StateMeaning
NewStarted, waiting for its turn.
RunRunning now.
SleepWaiting for a Wait step's time or a human task. It continues by itself.
CompletedFinished without errors.
ErrorA step failed. The error says which and why.
CancelledKilled by someone. The error says who.

Killing a run

To stop a run that is new, running or sleeping, select it and click the red stop icon, then confirm. You need to be allowed to edit the workflow. The run becomes Cancelled. A run in the daemon stops at once. One inside a web request stops when its current step ends. Long runs can also be killed from the Overview.

Cleaning up

Executions of the draft, from Run, can be deleted from the panel, one at a time or all at once. Executions of published versions, and those still running or sleeping, are kept. Their lines in the execution log stay in any case.

The execution log

Besides each workflow's executions, the account keeps an execution log of all runs and of the requests refused by triggers, such as a webhook call with a wrong secret. Owners find it in the Settings menu under System execution log. How long entries are kept is an account setting.

The Overview page shows the runs of the last days, with how many completed and how many failed.

pages.title: Overview
pages.summary: The project's dashboard: how its workflows run, what failed, what is running and waiting.
pages.html:
The Overview, at the top of the sidebar, is the current project's dashboard. It shows how the project's workflows run.

Period

Choose 24h, 7d, 30d or 90d at the top. Everything below follows the period, and each figure is compared with the period before. Your browser remembers the choice.

What it shows

  • Figures: the executions, the success rate, the median run time, what is running now and what is waiting (sleeping runs), and the open tasks.
  • Executions over time: completed and failed runs, per hour or per day.
  • Executions by trigger: how runs were started: schedule, webhook, form, file upload, email, manual.
  • Run time by workflow: the median run time of each workflow, up to its slowest runs (95th percentile).
  • Workflows: a sortable table of the workflows, with their last run and a small chart of their runs.
  • Problems: the steps that fail most, and work that seems stuck. A run still going after 15 minutes has a Kill button (if you may edit its workflow). Killing stops the run, and it shows as Cancelled. A run in the daemon stops at once. One inside a web request stops when its current step ends.
  • Recent executions: the latest runs.

Click Refresh to update the figures. To see one run in detail, open its workflow's Executions panel.

pages.title: Projects and members
pages.summary: Creating projects, switching between them, managing who is a member, and moving work to another server.
pages.html:
A project holds related work: workflows, credentials and variables, data tables and files. Only its members see what is inside.

Your personal project

Every user has a project called Personal, created the first time they sign in. Only they are a member of it, which makes it a good place to try things.

Switching projects

The current project's name is at the top of the sidebar. Click it to switch to another project you belong to. The sidebar then shows that project's workflows, credentials, tables and files.

Creating a project

Click + at the top of the sidebar and choose New project. You become its owner. Your role must allow creating projects.

Project settings

Click the gear icon at the top of the sidebar to open the current project's settings. It has these tabs:

  • General: the project's icon and name.
  • Members: who is in the project, and with which role.
  • Export / import: move workflows, credentials and data tables to another NetFlow9 server. Shown to roles that may export and import (Owner by default).

Members

  • Add a member: choose a user of the account and a role.
  • Invite by email: an address that is already a user of the account is added at once. Any other address receives a link to join. Pending invitations are listed with Resend and Cancel.
  • Change a role: choose another role in the member's row. The change is saved right away.
  • Remove: takes the user out of the project. The last member with the Owner role cannot be removed or changed.

A member's role in the project decides what they may do in it, for example build workflows (Member) or only fill in forms and complete tasks (Participant). See Roles and permissions.

A personal project has no other members.

Moving work to another server

To move work between NetFlow9 servers, for example from development to pre-production, export it to a file on one server and import that file into a project on the other.

Export

  • Tick the workflows, credentials and variables, and data tables to include. Also the credentials and data tables the chosen workflows use adds what their steps need.
  • Tick with rows on a data table to include its data. Otherwise only its columns are exported.
  • Workflows are exported as their drafts: the steps as last saved in the designer.
  • Passphrase: with one, the file is encrypted and includes the credentials' secrets (passwords, keys, tokens). Without one, the file has no secrets, and you enter them again after the import. Each server encrypts secrets with its own key, so the two servers do not need the same APP_SECRET.

Import

Choose the file and enter its passphrase, if it has one. The next page lists everything in the file. Items are matched to this project's by name, and for each one you choose what to do:

ItemNot in the projectAlready in the project
Data tableCreateUpdate its columns and keep its rows (default); update its columns and replace its rows (if the file has rows); create a copy; skip
CredentialCreateSkip and keep this server's (default); replace it; create a copy
WorkflowCreateReplace its draft (default); create a copy; skip

Nothing changes until you click Import. Then:

  • Steps are pointed at this server's credentials and data tables: the imported ones, or the ones of the same name already in the project. The import page warns about anything the steps use that is in neither the file nor the project.
  • Imported workflows are drafts. Check them in the designer, then publish them. A replaced workflow that was published keeps running its live version until you publish the new draft.
  • Webhook, form and email triggers keep their token, so on the new server their URL differs only in the host name. A replaced workflow keeps the URLs it already had. If another workflow on the server already uses a token, the step gets a new one.
  • Columns that exist on both sides are updated. Columns only on this server are kept, with their data.
  • OAuth credentials need this server's redirect URI added to the app at the provider. Then use Connect again.

Files, executions, published versions and user assignments (for example a task's assignee) are not exported. Each export and import is recorded in the audit log.

pages.title: Forms
pages.summary: The list of the forms people can fill in, and how forms are shared.
pages.html:
Forms, in the sidebar, lists the forms of the account's published workflows that you can open: one per Form trigger. Click one to fill it in. Sending it starts its workflow.

When the list is empty, no published workflow has a Form trigger yet. Add one to a workflow and publish it.

Sharing a form

Each form has its own address, shown in the Form trigger's settings. What happens when someone opens it depends on the trigger's Who can fill it in:

  • Project members (logged in): visitors are asked to sign in, then come back to the form.
  • Anyone with the link: no sign-in, so customers or partners can fill it in.

After sending, the visitor sees the trigger's Message after sending.

pages.title: My tasks
pages.summary: The tasks assigned to you by workflows, and how to complete them.
pages.html:
My tasks, in the sidebar, lists the open tasks assigned to you by Human task steps. A badge shows how many there are. Tasks come from all the account's projects you belong to.

Completing a task

  1. Click a task to open it. You see its instructions and its form.
  2. Fill in the form and press the button, for example Complete or Approve.
  3. The workflow that was waiting continues with your answers.

A task assigned to a role or to several people can be completed by any of them. Once someone has completed it, it leaves everyone's list. If a task reaches its time limit first, it expires and can no longer be completed. Opening it then says "This task is no longer open."

Note: users with the Participant role see Forms and My tasks. They don't see the workflows.

pages.title: Data tables
pages.summary: Simple tables inside NetFlow9: columns, rows, importing CSV or Excel, and using them in workflows.
pages.html:
Data tables are simple tables kept inside NetFlow9, one set per project. Workflows read and write them with the Data Table step, and you can browse and edit them by hand. Use them for lists of customers, processed orders, settings, logs of what a workflow did, and so on.

Creating a table

Open Data Tables in the sidebar. Create an empty table and add its columns, or Import a file to create the table from it.

Columns

SettingDescription
LabelThe column's title.
KeyIts name in workflows: {{ table.rows[0].email }}. Letters, digits or underscore, not starting with a digit. It cannot be changed later.
TypeText, Textarea, Number, Email, Url, Checkbox, Switch, Datetime, Date, Select (a list of choices, one per line) or Object (points to a user, a file, or a row of another table). It cannot be changed later.
RequiredRows must have a value in this column.

Each row also has an id, and the times it was created and last updated (created_at, updated_at).

Rows

Add, edit and delete rows on the table's page. The grid can be sorted and filtered. Values are checked against the columns' types and rules, both by hand and from workflows.

Importing CSV or Excel

  1. Click Import and choose a .csv, .tsv, .txt or .xlsx file.
  2. In the preview, give the table a name, choose the sheet (Excel) and whether the first row is a header.
  3. Check the columns found: import each one or not, and set its name, key and type. The types are guessed from the values. The first rows are shown as they will be read.
  4. Click Import.

Limits

Your plan may limit the number of tables and the rows in one table. The Usage page shows where you stand.

AI steps can also work with data tables when you allow their tools: list and query tables, and insert, update or delete rows. See AI steps.

pages.title: Files
pages.summary: The project's files: uploading, previewing, and using them in workflows.
pages.html:
Files, in the sidebar, holds the project's files: those you upload, and those saved by workflows, such as email attachments, downloads and FTP files.

Uploading

Drag files onto the list, or use the upload button. These types are accepted:

KindExtensions
Imagepng, jpg, jpeg, gif, webp, bmp, tif, tiff, svg, heic
PDFpdf
Word, Documentdoc, docx, odt, rtf
Excel, Spreadsheet, CSVxls, xlsx, ods, csv, tsv
PowerPoint, Presentationppt, pptx, odp
Text, Markdown, HTMLtxt, log, md, html, htm
JSON, XML, YAMLjson, xml, yaml, yml

The largest file depends on the server's settings. Your plan may limit the space used by all files.

Previewing and downloading

Click a file to open its page. Images, PDF, Word and Excel files are shown in the page. Every file can be downloaded.

Files in workflows

  • A File upload trigger starts a workflow when a file is uploaded.
  • Steps that save files give their id: {{ file.id }} (Download File), {{ mail.attachment_files }}, {{ ftp.files }}.
  • Steps that use files take these ids: email attachments and images, AI step files, FTP / SFTP Upload, Google Drive and OneDrive uploads.

pages.title: Credentials & variables
pages.summary: Storing passwords, API keys and OAuth connections for the steps, and the project's shared variables.
pages.html:
Credentials & variables, in the sidebar, holds what the project's steps need to connect to other systems, and the values its workflows share.

  • Credentials are stored encrypted. After saving, secret fields are not shown again. Leave them empty when editing to keep the saved value.
  • Steps refer to a credential by name, so a workflow never contains a secret.
  • A credential belongs to one project, and only that project's workflows can use it.

Kinds of credentials

GroupCredentialUsed by
HTTPAPI key, Basic auth, Bearer tokenHTTP Request, Download File
AIAnthropic (Claude), OpenAI API (or compatible server), Google Gemini, Ollama server, Lemonade serverThe AI steps
AIMCP serverAI steps (the tools of an external MCP server)
EmailIMAP server (password), Google Mail (OAuth), Microsoft 365 Mail (OAuth)Read emails (IMAP); Google Mail also for Gmail
FilesFTP / SFTP serverFTP / SFTP, FTP / SFTP Upload
FilesDecryption key, Verification key, Encryption key, Signing keyDecrypting, checking signatures, encrypting and signing files in the FTP steps (PGP / GPG, OpenSSL, S/MIME)
GoogleGoogle Drive, Sheets, Calendar, Docs (OAuth)The Google steps
MicrosoftOutlook Mail, Outlook Calendar, OneDrive & SharePoint, Microsoft Teams (Microsoft Graph)The Microsoft 365 steps
DatabaseMySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, Firebird, ODBC data sourceThe Database step
DirectoriesLDAP serverThe LDAP step
OtherVariableAny expression, as {{ vars.<name> }}

Kinds that depend on the installation, such as the databases, appear only when available.

Testing

Most credentials have a Test button that tries the connection and shows the result. AI server credentials also record the models the server offers, so the AI steps can list them. The list shows when each credential was last tested and used.

OAuth credentials (Google, Microsoft)

OAuth credentials connect with an OAuth app that you register at the provider. Step-by-step guides: Google and Microsoft 365. In short:

  1. Create a web application OAuth app at the provider and enable the APIs you need, such as the Gmail API or Microsoft Graph permissions.
  2. Add the Redirect URI shown in the credential's form to the app.
  3. Copy the app's Client ID and Client secret into the credential and save.
  4. Click Connect. You are sent to the provider to sign in and consent, then back. Account then shows who the credential acts as.

NetFlow9 renews the access token by itself. If the consent is withdrawn at the provider, connect again.

Project variables

A credential of kind Variable is a shared value: a base URL, a team's address, a threshold. Its name must be a valid identifier. Every workflow of the project reads it as {{ vars.<name> }}, and its Description appears in the expression suggestions. Change the value once, and every workflow uses the new one at its next run.

pages.title: The Assistant
pages.summary: Building and changing workflows by describing them in your own words.
pages.html:
The Assistant builds workflows for you. Describe what you want in plain words, and it adds and connects the steps, fills in their settings, and explains what it did. You see the changes on the canvas as they happen. It is part of NetFlow9 itself, on every plan, Free included.

Using it

  1. In the designer, click the Assistant button (the stars icon) in the toolbar. The panel opens on the right.
  2. Describe the workflow or the change, for example:
    • "Every morning at 8, get yesterday's orders from https://shop.example.com/api/orders and email a summary to sales@example.com."
    • "Add an error output to the HTTP request that notifies me by email."
    • "Why does this workflow fail at the If step?"
  3. Press Send, or Stop to interrupt it.

Changes are saved like your own. If you don't like a change, press Ctrl+Z to undo it. Each workflow keeps its conversation with the Assistant.

Note: the Assistant uses the credentials and tables that exist in the project. It cannot create credentials: add them yourself, then ask it to use them.

Settings

An owner sets up the Assistant under Settings → Assistant:

SettingDescription
ProviderWho runs the Assistant: System AI (provided by this installation, when it has one, paid with the account's AI credits), or your own account with Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI (or a compatible server), Google Gemini, Ollama or a Lemonade server (your key, your costs).
Server URL, API keyFor your own provider. The URL is empty for the provider's own API, or a proxy or local server.
ModelConnect to list the server's models.
EffortHow thoroughly Claude thinks: higher is better for large workflows, lower is faster and cheaper.
Monthly budget (USD)The most the Assistant may spend per calendar month, with your own key. Empty or 0: no limit.
Monthly credit limitWith the System AI: the Assistant stops once the credits the account used this month (by the Assistant and the AI steps) reach it.
Input / Output priceThe prices the budget is counted with (USD per million tokens). Empty: the known prices of Claude models.

When the Assistant isn't set up yet, its panel says so and links to these settings.

pages.title: Signing in
pages.summary: The sign-in page, remember me, several accounts, forgotten passwords, two-factor codes and single sign-on.
pages.html:
Sign in with your email address and password. Depending on your account's settings, you may also sign in with your company directory (LDAP) or your identity provider (SSO).

The sign-in page

  • Remember me: stay signed in after closing the browser. Without it, closing the browser signs you out.
  • Several accounts: if your address is a user of more than one NetFlow9 account, you choose which one after signing in.
  • Two-factor code: if you activated two-factor authentication, you are asked for the code from your authenticator app.
  • Sign in with SSO: when your account uses SAML single sign-on, type your email. You are sent to your identity provider and back.

Forgot your password

Click Forgot username or password? and type your email. You receive a link to choose a new password, valid for a limited time. Setting a new password signs you out everywhere else.

Users who sign in with LDAP or SSO have no NetFlow9 password: they change it in their directory or identity provider.

Being signed out

Your account may sign you out after a period of inactivity, and after a maximum session length. Both are set by an owner in Account settings.

pages.title: Your profile and two-factor authentication
pages.summary: Your name and email, changing your password, and protecting your sign-in with an authenticator app.
pages.html:
Open your profile from the sidebar: click your name at the bottom, then Personal.

Basic information

Your first name, last name and email. Your role is set by an owner, so you cannot change it here.

Password

Click Change to set a new password. You type your current password, then the new one twice.

Two-factor authentication (2FA)

With 2FA, signing in also asks for a 6-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone, such as Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password or Authy. Someone who learns your password still cannot sign in.

  1. In Security, choose to activate two-factor authentication.
  2. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, or type the key it shows.
  3. Type the code the app shows now, then click Activate.

To turn it off, deactivate it in the same place. It asks for a current code.

Warning: when your account enforces MFA, you must activate 2FA before you can use the app. The profile page says so, and you cannot turn it off.

pages.title: Users
pages.summary: The account's users: adding people, roles and states.
pages.html:
Users, in the Settings menu, lists the people of the account. Only users who may see all the account's users have this page, which by default means owners.

Adding people

There are two ways:

  • Invite them to a project (recommended): in the project's settings, Members → Invite by email. They receive a link, choose their name and password, and join the account as Members of that project. See Projects and members.
  • Create a user: on the Users page, click Create and give their first name, last name, email and role. They receive an email with a link to choose their password, valid once for 7 days.

With LDAP or SAML sign-in, users can also be created automatically the first time they sign in. See LDAP sign-in and SAML single sign-on.

Editing a user

Click a user, or Edit in their row's menu, to change their first name, last name, email, role and state.

  • Send sign-in link emails them a new link to choose a password, for example when the first one expired or they lost access. It is offered for active users who sign in with a NetFlow9 password (not LDAP or SSO users).
  • Setting a user to Disabled signs them out everywhere at once.
  • The account always keeps an active Owner: the last one cannot be given another role or disabled. Give someone else the Owner role first.
  • Your own user opens your profile: you cannot change your own role or state.

Roles

Each user has an account role: Owner, Member, Participant, or a role you create. It decides what they may do across the account. In each project, a member also has a project role. See Roles and permissions.

States

StateMeaning
ActiveCan sign in.
UnconfirmedSigned up but has not confirmed their email yet.
DisabledCannot sign in.

pages.title: Roles and permissions
pages.summary: The built-in roles, creating your own, and what each permission and scope allows.
pages.html:
What a user may do comes from their role. A role is a list of permissions, each with a scope.

The built-in roles

RoleFor
OwnerThe people who run the account: everything, including account settings, users, roles, logs and usage.
MemberThe people who build: workflows, credentials, data tables and files in the projects they belong to. They see only their own user, and cannot change the account's settings.
ParticipantThe people who take part: they fill in the project's forms and complete the tasks assigned to them, and see no workflows.

Some permissions of the built-in roles are locked so that an account cannot lock itself out. They are shown greyed out.

Creating and editing roles

Open Roles in the Settings menu. Create a role, or open one to edit its permissions. For each permission, tick it to allow it and choose its scope, then Save.

Scopes

ScopeAllows the permission on
globalEverything in the account.
projectWhat belongs to the projects the user is a member of.
ownThe user's own record only (their profile, their password).

Permissions

AreaPermissionsScopes
AccountUpdate account settings; view the account's usage and its plan's limitsglobal
UsersCreate, view (and list), edit, delete users; change passwordglobal (edit, change password: also own)
ProjectsCreate, view (and list), edit, delete projects; export and import workflows, credentials (with their secrets) and data tables (Owner only by default)global
RolesCreate, view (and list), edit, delete rolesglobal
WorkflowsCreate, view (and list), edit, delete workflows; publish and unpublishglobal, project
CredentialsCreate, view (and list; secrets are never shown), edit / test / connect, deleteglobal, project
Data tablesCreate, view the columns (and list), edit the columns, delete tables; view the data; change the dataglobal, project
FilesCreate (upload), view (and list), edit, deleteglobal, project
LogsView the audit log; view the execution log (project scope: the entries of the user's projects)global, project
MCP server tokensCreate, view (and list), delete (revoke)global, project

"View" also allows listing. For example, a role that may view workflows in project scope sees the workflows of its projects in the sidebar.

Project roles

In a project, each member has a role for that project. For permissions with project scope, the project role applies to what is inside the project. So the same person can be a Member in one project and a Participant in another.

pages.title: Account settings
pages.summary: Security (MFA, session limits), how long logs are kept, and date formats.
pages.html:
Account settings, in the Settings menu, apply to every user of the account. Only users who may update the account see this page.

Security

SettingDescription
Enforce MFAEvery user must activate two-factor authentication. Until they do, they can only reach their profile, to set it up.

Sessions

SettingChoices
Sign out after inactivity15 minutes; 30 minutes (default); 1 hour; 4 hours; 24 hours
Maximum session length8 hours; 12 hours (default); 24 hours; 7 days; 30 days. Counted from signing in.

The limits apply to every session, including Remember me sign-ins. Those differ only in staying signed in after the browser is closed.

Logs

SettingChoices
Keep audit log entriesForever (default); 1 year; 2 years; 3 years
Keep execution log entriesForever; 30 days; 90 days (default); 1 year

A shorter time also removes the older entries already written. Audit log entries are kept at least 1 year.

Dates

Date format and Date and time format set how dates are shown across the app, in lists, fields and date pickers. Each choice is shown with an example. Default uses the installation's format.

Other settings pages

Depending on what your installation provides and your plan, the Settings menu also has:

  • LDAP sign-in and SAML single sign-on
  • Inbound mail: the email prefix of the Email (inbound) trigger
  • Assistant: who runs the designer's Assistant
  • Usage and AI credits

pages.title: LDAP sign-in
pages.summary: Letting people sign in with their directory password (Active Directory, OpenLDAP...), with roles from their groups.
pages.html:
With LDAP sign-in, the people of your account sign in with their directory user name and password, such as Active Directory or OpenLDAP. Their role in NetFlow9 comes from their directory groups, checked at every sign-in. Other users keep their own NetFlow9 password. This feature depends on your plan.

Set it up under Settings → LDAP sign-in.

The server

SettingDescription
DirectoryThe kind of directory, such as Active Directory or OpenLDAP. Sets the usual attribute names and filters, each of which can be changed.
ServersHost names or IP addresses, optionally with :port, separated by commas. Tried in order until one answers.
PortEmpty: 636 for LDAPS, else 389.
EncryptionPasswords are sent to the server, so use None only on a trusted network.
Check the server's certificateTurn it off only for a test server. Without the check, anyone on the way can read the passwords.
CA certificateOptional: the certificate (PEM) of the authority that signed the server's, when it is not a public one, such as your company's CA.
Bind DN, Bind passwordThe account that reads the directory, e.g. CN=svc-netflow,OU=Service,DC=example,DC=com. Active Directory also takes svc-netflow@example.com. Empty: anonymous.
Base DNWhere searches start, e.g. DC=example,DC=com.

Finding people

SettingDescription
User filterFinds the person by the name typed at sign-in, written as {login}. Empty: the directory's usual filter, which is shown.
Name, email, first name, last name attributesEmpty: sAMAccountName / uid, mail, givenName, sn.
Groups fromRead memberOf, or search the groups. OpenLDAP shows memberOf only with its memberof overlay.
Group base DN, Group filterWhere and how to search a person's groups: {dn} is the person's DN, {login} the name attribute's value.

Groups and roles

A list of rows, each a directory group and a NetFlow9 role. A person gets the role of the first row whose group they are in, so put the most powerful groups first. Others is the role for people in none of the groups. Leave it empty to refuse their sign-in.

Users

SettingDescription
Create users on their first sign-inOff: only users already linked to the directory can sign in.
Link existing usersA user of the account whose email matches a directory person's signs in with LDAP from then on, and no longer with their NetFlow9 password.
Email domainsSomeone signing in as name@domain without a user yet is looked up in this directory when the domain is one of these.
Names without @domain are this directory'sA name such as jdoe, with no user yet, is looked up in this directory. At most one account of the installation can use this.

Use Test before turning sign-in on: it checks the connection, or tries a sign-in with a user name and password and shows the person found and the role they would get. LDAP users have no password to reset in NetFlow9. Two-factor authentication still applies if they activate it or the account enforces it.

Note: workflows reach a directory with the LDAP step and an LDAP server credential. That is separate from sign-in, and every account has it, whatever its plan.

pages.title: SAML single sign-on
pages.summary: Signing in through your identity provider (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, ADFS, Keycloak...).
pages.html:
With SAML single sign-on, the people of your account sign in at your identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, ADFS or Keycloak. NetFlow9 trusts the IdP's answer and gives them the role of their IdP groups. Other users keep their own password. This feature depends on your plan.

Set it up under Settings → SAML single sign-on.

Setting it up

  1. In your IdP, create a SAML application for NetFlow9. Give it the values shown on the settings page: this application's metadata URL, its entity ID and its reply (ACS) URL. Many IdPs can read them all from the metadata URL.
  2. Back in NetFlow9, paste the IdP's metadata URL and click Import. This fills in the IdP's entity ID, sign-on URL and signing certificates. You can also type them.
  3. Map the IdP's groups to roles (below).
  4. Click Test to try a sign-in, then turn on Sign in with SAML single sign-on.

Settings

SettingDescription
IdP entity ID, single sign-on URL, signing certificatesFrom the IdP. Several certificates are allowed during a rollover. Responses must be signed by one of them.
Service provider entity IDEmpty: this application's metadata URL.
NameID formatWhat identifies a person. Users are found by it, then by email.
Sign the requestsSign-in requests are signed with this application's certificate.
Assertions must be encryptedWith this application's certificate, published in its metadata.
Ask the IdP to sign in againForceAuthn: no single sign-on with the IdP's existing session.
Accept IdP-initiated sign-insFrom the IdP's portal (an app tile), without a request from NetFlow9. Less safe: the response is not tied to the browser that asked.
Email, groups, first name, last name attributesEmpty: the usual names (email, mail, groups, memberOf, givenName, sn…).
Groups and roles; OthersAs for LDAP: the role of the first row whose group the person has, with the group as the IdP sends it (a name, an ID, a DN). Others: the role of everyone else. Empty refuses them.
Create users on their first sign-in; Link existing users; Email domainsAs for LDAP. A linked user signs in only at the IdP from then on, and their NetFlow9 password is removed.
Ask this application's 2FA tooOff: the IdP's sign-in is enough, and it usually asks its own MFA. On: users with 2FA in NetFlow9 also give its code.

This application's certificate can be renewed from the settings page. Publish the new metadata to the IdP when you do.

Signing in

People click Sign in with SSO on the sign-in page and type their email. The account is found by its email domain, and they are sent to the IdP. Signing out of NetFlow9 ends the NetFlow9 session only, not the IdP's.

pages.title: Inbound mail
pages.summary: The email prefix of your account's Email (inbound) trigger addresses.
pages.html:
Each Email (inbound) step has its own address, such as acme-7f3k2m9q@in.example.com. The first part is your account's email prefix, set under Settings → Inbound mail.

SettingDescription
Email prefixThe start of your inbound addresses (prefix-xxxxxxxx@domain). Changing it changes all of them, so update any system that sends to the old addresses.

This page appears only when the installation receives mail. On a self-hosted installation, see Inbound mail.

pages.title: Usage and AI credits
pages.summary: What the account uses of its plan's limits, and its System AI credits.
pages.html:
Usage

Usage, in the Settings menu, shows what the account uses of its plan's limits. The limits are for the whole account:

  • Data tables: how many there are, the largest table, and the tables close to the row limit.
  • Files: the space used by all files.
  • AI credits: used this month.
  • Features: what the plan includes, such as LDAP sign-in and SAML.
  • Per project: each project's share.

When a limit is reached, the action that would go over it is refused with a message: creating a table, adding rows, uploading a file, or an AI call on the System AI.

AI credits

When the installation offers a System AI, its use is paid with the account's credits: by the Assistant with the System provider, and by AI steps whose credential is System AI. Settings → AI credits shows:

  • The monthly allowance: credits given each month. Unused credits don't roll over.
  • Top-ups: extra credits, used after the allowance and valid for 12 months.
  • What was used this month, and the latest changes, with their balance.

Each AI call counts its tokens in credits according to the model. A run reserves credits before calling the model, stops before a call once its credits are used up, and is charged only what it used.

pages.title: Audit and execution logs
pages.summary: Who did what in the account, and the record of all workflow runs.
pages.html:
The audit log

The audit log records who did what, and when: sign-ins, changes to users, roles and settings, and the creation, change, publishing and deletion of workflows, credentials, tables and files. Each entry shows who acted, from which address, what changed, and the values before and after. Secrets are never logged.

Owners find the whole account's log in the Settings menu under System audit log. Users whose role allows the audit log in project scope see the entries of their projects.

Click an entry to see its details. The list can be filtered and sorted.

The execution log

The execution log records the runs of all workflows: when, which workflow and version, what started it and how it ended. It also records requests refused by triggers, such as a webhook call with a wrong secret or to an unpublished workflow. Owners find it in the Settings menu under System execution log.

For the details of one run (its log lines and variables), open the workflow's Executions panel.

Retention

How long each log keeps its entries is set in Account settings. Audit entries are kept at least one year.

pages.title: Plugins overview
pages.summary: The optional features of NetFlow9, what each adds, and how they are enabled.
pages.html:
Many features of NetFlow9 come as plugins: LDAP and SAML sign-in, inbound mail, the System AI, and more. On a hosted installation they are managed for you. Whether you see a plugin's features depends on your plan and on what the installation provides. The Google and Microsoft 365 steps, the Assistant and the MCP server are not plugins: they are part of NetFlow9 itself, on every plan, Free included.

PluginAddsDepends on
LDAPSign-in with a directory (the LDAP step and credential are built in)Plan feature ldap
SAMLSingle sign-on through an identity providerPlan feature saml
Inbound mailThe Email (inbound) triggerThe installation receives mail (Haraka)
System AIAn AI model offered by the installation, paid with creditsThe installation's settings
Tool serversTools the installation runs for AI steps, such as a web browserEnabled per account by the administrator
AdministrationThe super-admins' pages: services, accounts, plansSuper-admins
RegistrationThe sign-up page: new accountsNone

Self-hosted installations

Plugins are folders in app/plugins/. They are enabled by listing them in app/plugins.php, in this order (some use others): Admin, Registration, SystemAI, InboundMail, Ldap, Saml, LocalMCP. Remove a name to turn the plugin off: its menus, steps, credentials and pages disappear. Its data stays in the database.

To write your own plugin, see Plugins and hooks.

pages.title: LDAP
pages.summary: Directory sign-in and the LDAP step.
pages.html:
The LDAP plugin connects NetFlow9 to a directory such as Active Directory or OpenLDAP, in two separate ways:

  • Sign-in: people sign in with their directory password, with roles from their groups. Set it up under Settings → LDAP sign-in. See LDAP sign-in.
  • Workflows: the LDAP server credential and the LDAP step search and manage entries, groups and passwords.

The plugin is the sign-in, and depends on the plan feature ldap. The LDAP server credential and the LDAP step are part of NetFlow9 itself: every account has them, whatever its plan, and they work with the plugin turned off. On a self-hosted installation, the PHP ldap extension is used when present. Otherwise NetFlow9 uses its own client.

pages.title: SAML
pages.summary: Single sign-on through your identity provider.
pages.html:
The SAML plugin lets the people of an account sign in at their identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, ADFS or Keycloak, with roles from their groups. The sign-in page gets a Sign in with SSO link. Set it up under Settings → SAML single sign-on. See SAML single sign-on.

It depends on the plan feature saml. It is for sign-in only: it adds no steps or credentials.

pages.title: Inbound mail
pages.summary: The Email (inbound) trigger: workflows started by email.
pages.html:
The Inbound mail plugin adds the Email (inbound) trigger, which gives each workflow its own email address, and the account's email prefix setting.

It is active only when the installation receives mail through Haraka. Without it, the trigger and its settings don't appear. To set it up on your own server, see Inbound mail.

pages.title: System AI
pages.summary: An AI model offered by the installation, paid with credits.
pages.html: The System AI plugin offers an AI model run by the installation to every account. AI steps can use it as their credential, and the Assistant as its provider, without an API key of your own. Use is paid in AI credits: a monthly allowance plus top-ups, shown under Settings → AI credits. See Usage and AI credits, and for self-hosted installations System AI.

pages.title: Tool servers
pages.summary: Tools the installation runs for AI steps.
pages.html: The Tool servers plugin offers MCP servers that run on the installation to the AI steps of the accounts the administrator enables. The first is a sandboxed web browser: the model can open pages, read them and fill in forms. Enabled accounts see it under Tool servers in their AI steps. See AI steps, and for self-hosted installations Tool servers.

pages.title: Administration
pages.summary: The super-admins' pages.
pages.html: The Administration plugin adds Settings → Administration for super-admins. There they manage the installation's services, all the accounts with their plans, limits, credits and tool servers, and can suspend or view an account. See Administration.

pages.title: Registration
pages.summary: The sign-up page for new accounts.
pages.html: The Registration plugin adds a sign-up link to the sign-in page, so people can create a new account themselves. They enter their email and receive a confirmation link. The link's page asks for the account's name (their company or team), their name and a password. They become the new account's Owner. Without the plugin, there is no sign-up page.

pages.title: Requirements
pages.summary: What a server needs to run NetFlow9: PHP and its extensions, MongoDB, a web server, and optional tools.
pages.html:
NetFlow9 runs on a Linux server with PHP, MongoDB and a web server (nginx with PHP-FPM). On AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux or RHEL 9, the installer installs all of them. The installer (install.sh in the app's folder, or the setup in the browser) checks all of this before installing, and tells you what is missing.

Required

ComponentVersion / details
PHP8.1 or later, for the web server (PHP-FPM) and on the command line (/usr/bin/php, same version: the daemon runs the workflows)
PHP extension mongodb2.3.0 or later. The MongoDB PHP library ships with NetFlow9 (in app/pkgs).
PHP extensionsopenssl (encrypted credentials, TLS), mbstring, curl (HTTP and AI steps, OAuth), json, iconv, simplexml and zip (Excel import), ctype, session
PCRE10.30 or later, with Unicode (bundled with modern PHP)
Command-line PHP extensionspcntl and posix (the daemon)
MongoDBA server or replica set reachable from the app, with a database for NetFlow9
Web servernginx with PHP-FPM, HTTPS
SMTP serverTo send emails: sign-in links, invitations, the Send email step

These folders must be writable by the app's user: the app's folder itself (the setup writes app.env there), logs, tmp, run and var.

Recommended

ComponentFor
PHP extensions zlib, bz2The FTP / SFTP steps: .gz compression, .bz2 decompression
curl with ftp, ftps, sftpThe FTP / SFTP steps (SFTP needs curl built with libssh)
gpg, openssl programsThe FTP / SFTP steps: PGP and S/MIME encryption and signatures
PHP extension ldapLDAP sign-in and the LDAP step. NetFlow9 has its own client when the extension is missing.
PHP extensions pdo_mysql, pdo_pgsql, pdo_sqlsrv or pdo_dblib, pdo_oci, pdo_firebird, pdo_odbcThe Database step: the extension of each kind of database it connects to, in the web and the command-line PHP. See Database.
Node.jsInbound mail (Haraka) and the web browser tool server (Playwright)
systemd and polkitRunning the daemon and the other services, and managing them from the administration pages (minimal systems may not have polkit: dnf install polkit)

Without the recommended parts, NetFlow9 runs. Only the steps that need them fail when used.

pages.title: Installation
pages.summary: Installing NetFlow9: the installer (install.sh) sets up the server and the app on RHEL 9 and its kin; or by hand, with the setup in the browser.
pages.html:
On AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux or RHEL 9, the installer sets up the whole server: the packages, the app's user, the app itself, the web server, and the options. Run it as root, from any folder:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/netflow9/netflow9/main/install.sh
sudo bash install.sh

1. What it asks

  • The server: the site's domain (its DNS record points to the server), the system user NetFlow9 runs as (its home, such as /home/app, holds the app), and the repository and branch to install from.
  • Options: MongoDB on this server (otherwise you give the connection string of yours), a Let's Encrypt certificate (offered when the domain points to the server; otherwise a self-signed one), the web browser for the AI steps, inbound email and its domain, securing MongoDB (its own users with random passwords, sign-in required), and SELinux permissive when it is enforcing (nginx and PHP-FPM serve the app from the user's home).

It then shows what it will do and asks to go on.

2. What it does

  1. Installs the packages that are missing: EPEL, PHP 8.5 (Remi) with the app's extensions and the Database step's drivers (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Firebird, ODBC; Oracle's needs Oracle's Instant Client, installed by hand), nginx, MongoDB 8.3, Redis, certbot, and Node.js (the newest stream of the distribution; for the web browser and inbound email).
  2. Creates the user and its home, and clones the repository there, with its submodules (the libraries in app/pkgs).
  3. Writes php.ini (with the server's time zone), the app's PHP-FPM pool and the logrotate configuration (templates in scripts/system/), the certificate, and the nginx site.
  4. Sets up the app. It asks:
    • the database name (a new or empty one), and the MongoDB connection string when MongoDB is elsewhere;
    • the outgoing email: SMTP server, port, encryption (none, TLS, SSL), username and password, and the sender address;
    • the first account: the company or team, and its owner: username, email, first and last name, password.
    The app checks the answers itself: a wrong one, or a database that cannot be reached or already has an account, is asked again. It then creates the database indexes, the account with its roles (Owner, Member, Participant) and its owner, and writes app.env with a new random APP_SECRET.
  5. Installs the options and the background services (the workflow daemon, and Haraka and the web browser when chosen).

The firewall is not changed: open ports 80 and 443, and 25 for inbound email. Open the site and sign in with the owner you created. Run the installer again (sudo bash /home/<user>/install.sh) to add an option later, or for Let's Encrypt once the domain points to the server: the app's settings and account are kept, and what is done is left as it is.

Warning: keep a copy of app.env in a safe place. Its APP_SECRET encrypts the stored credentials. Without it they cannot be read.

The app's folder

/home/app
  app/            the application (PHP); app/pkgs: the libraries (git submodules)
  public_html/    the web root (index.php, css, js)
  install.sh      the installer
  scripts/        its parts and the service scripts; nginx/ and system/: the templates
  etc/            links to the app's nginx site and PHP-FPM pool
  ssl/            the certificate (ssl.crt, ssl.key)
  logs/ tmp/ run/ var/    written by the app

Or: by hand

On another system, install PHP 8.1 or later with the required extensions, MongoDB, nginx with a PHP-FPM pool running as the app's user (see nginx and PHP-FPM), and polkit. Clone the app into the user's home with its submodules:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/netflow9/netflow9.git /home/app

(In a clone made without --recurse-submodules, fetch them with git submodule update --init.) Write the nginx site (there is no app.env yet, so give the host name), then open the site: as long as there is no app.env, every address shows the setup wizard.

sudo scripts/0_nginx-install.sh --server-name=netflow.example.com
  1. Prerequisites: the PHP versions and extensions (web and command line), PCRE, the writable folders, and the recommended tools. Fix what is marked as required, then continue.
  2. Server: the public address, the MongoDB connection string and database name (the connection is tested here, and the database must not hold an account yet), and the outgoing email.
  3. Account: the first account and its owner.

Then install the options and the services with the scripts below (on RHEL 9 and its kin, sudo bash install.sh does it: it keeps the settings the wizard wrote).

The installer's parts

After the server's packages, user, files and PHP-FPM, the installer runs these scripts, in this order. Each can also be run alone, as root:

ScriptInstalls
0_nginx-install.shThe app's nginx site, from scripts/nginx/app.conf (nginx and PHP-FPM)
1_playwright-install.shPlaywright and Chromium, for the AI steps' web browser (tool servers)
2_haraka-install.shHaraka, for inbound mail (needs app.env)
3_mongo-auth-setup.shMongoDB's users (security; needs app.env); the installer then turns on sign-in in /etc/mongod.conf
4_services-install.shThe systemd services: the daemon, Haraka and the web browser, when they are installed. Needs polkit.

The app's own setup (between the nginx site and the others) is app/v setup::install, run as the app's user. Then, as needed: the System AI, tool servers, and a super-admin.

Check

Run the check suite. It exercises the workflow engine, expressions, steps and integrations against your installation:

cd app/commands && ./CheckCommand.sh

It ends with all N checks passed, or lists what failed. Checks of services you have not set up (real FTP servers, an AI server) are skipped or fail, and say why.

pages.title: Configuration (app.env)
pages.summary: Every setting of the app.env file: addresses, database, email, security, limits, logging and the System AI.
pages.html:
NetFlow9 reads its settings from app.env in the app's folder. The installer (or the setup in the browser) writes it. Edit it to change a setting, then restart PHP-FPM and the daemon. The format is one NAME=value per line. Put a value in single quotes to keep it literal, for example a password with a $.

Warning: app.env holds passwords and the encryption secret. Keep it readable by the app's user only (chmod 600), and out of the web root.

Addresses and database

SettingDescription
BASEThe app's folder, e.g. /home/app.
BASE_URLThe public address, e.g. https://netflow.example.com. Links in emails, webhook and form addresses and the OAuth redirect URI use it, always as https://.
MONGO_URIThe MongoDB connection string, e.g. mongodb://user:password@db1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0.
MONGO_DBThe database name.

Outgoing email

SettingDescription
SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORTThe SMTP server.
SMTP_USERNAME, SMTP_PASSWORD, SMTP_AUTHIts sign-in.
SMTP_SECUREfalse, ssl or tls.
SMTP_AUTOTLSUse STARTTLS when the server offers it.
SMTP_DOMAINThe domain emails come from: noreply@<domain>, unless MAIL_FROM is set.
MAIL_FROMThe sender address of the app's emails and the Send email step.
ERRORS_EMAILWhere the errors of background jobs are emailed, besides the log. Empty: logged only.

Inbound email

SettingDescription
MAIL_INBOUND_DOMAINThe domain of the Email (inbound) trigger addresses. See Inbound mail.
HARAKA_DIRWhere Haraka is installed. Default: <app>/haraka.

Security and behaviour

SettingDescription
APP_SECRETThe key that encrypts credentials and secret fields. Generated by the setup. Never change or lose it: stored credentials would become unreadable.
APP_DEBUGtrue shows error details on the pages and turns on development-only endpoints. Default false. Never true on a public server.
LOG_LEVELThe least severe messages written to logs/app.log: ERROR, WARN, INFO (default) or DEBUG.
HTTP_STEPS_ALLOW_PRIVATEtrue lets the HTTP Request and Download File steps call this machine and private networks (localhost, 10.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x…). Default false: public addresses only, checked again on each redirect.
MAX_SYNC_EXECUTIONSRuns that execute inside a web request at the same time, per account: Run in the designer, webhooks, forms, human tasks. Over the limit, runs that must answer with their result (a webhook set to answer when finished) get 429, and the others are handed to the daemon. 0: no limit.
SYNC_EXECUTION_TIMEOUTSeconds a run executes inside a web request before the daemon continues it from where it got to (default 30). A webhook set to answer when finished then answers 202 with the state queued. A single step that runs longer than PHP's max_execution_time stops the run with an error. 0: never handed over.

System AI

The AI server this installation offers to every account. See System AI.

SettingDescription
SYSTEM_AI_PROVIDERanthropic, openai, gemini, ollama or lemonade. Empty: no System AI.
SYSTEM_AI_URLEmpty: the provider's own API. Otherwise a proxy or your server.
SYSTEM_AI_API_KEY, SYSTEM_AI_MODELThe key and the model. Empty model: no System AI.
SYSTEM_AI_EFFORTClaude's effort (default high).
SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_INPUT, SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_OUTPUTUSD per million tokens. Needed for models other than Claude's, whose prices are known.
SYSTEM_AI_MONTHLY_CREDITSThe credits every account gets each month (default 500, no rollover).
SYSTEM_AI_MAX_CREDITS_PER_REQUESTThe most one request may reserve (default 200; 0: no limit).

Other configuration files

Some settings live in PHP files of the app. Copy one to its .local.php name to change it: the local file is read instead, and updates don't overwrite it.

  • app/tiers.php: the plans (tiers), their limits and features.
  • app/plugins/SystemAI/credit_rates.php: the credits per model and the margin.
  • app/plugins/LocalMCP/servers.php: the tool servers.
  • app/plugins.php: the plugins that are enabled.

pages.title: nginx and PHP-FPM
pages.summary: Serving NetFlow9 with nginx and a PHP-FPM pool, with HTTPS and the security headers.
pages.html:
The nginx site is in scripts/nginx/app.conf, as a template that scripts/0_nginx-install.sh fills in (see below). The installer writes the PHP-FPM pool, php.ini and logrotate from scripts/system/; the app's etc/ folder links to the pool and the nginx site.

PHP-FPM pool

[app]
user = app
group = app
listen = /home/app/run/php-fpm.sock
listen.owner = nginx
listen.group = nginx
pm = dynamic
pm.max_children = 25
pm.start_servers = 5
pm.min_spare_servers = 2
pm.max_spare_servers = 10
slowlog = /home/app/logs/php-slow.log
php_admin_flag[log_errors] = on
php_value[session.save_path] = /home/app/var/php/session

The pool runs as the app's user, so it can write logs, tmp and var. Raise upload_max_filesize and post_max_size to the largest file you want to accept.

nginx

sudo scripts/0_nginx-install.sh [--server-name=netflow.example.com] [--dry-run]

It fills in the template with the app's folder and the host name of BASE_URL (app.env; before the setup wizard has written it, give --server-name), shows the changes, and writes it to /etc/nginx/conf.d/<user>.conf, named after the app's user (or where the app's etc/nginx.conf link points). The old file is kept as <user>.conf.bak-<time> and put back if nginx -t fails; otherwise nginx is reloaded. --dry-run only shows the changes.

The certificate goes in ssl/ssl.crt and ssl/ssl.key of the app's folder. /etc/nginx/nginx.conf stays as installed: it loads conf.d/*.conf. The essentials of the site, with /home/app as the app's folder:

server {
    server_name netflow.example.com;
    listen 80;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

server {
    server_name netflow.example.com;
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    ssl_certificate     /home/app/ssl/ssl.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /home/app/ssl/ssl.key;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

    root /home/app/public_html;
    index index.php;
    client_max_body_size 100M;
    fastcgi_read_timeout 600;

    access_log /home/app/logs/app_access.log;
    error_log  /home/app/logs/app_error.log;

    # static files: long cache, compressed
    location ~* \.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif|ico|css|js|woff2|woff|eot|svg|ttf|map)$ {
        gzip on;
        expires max;
    }
    location ~* \.mjs$ {
        types { text/javascript mjs; }
        gzip on;
        expires max;
    }

    location ~ \.php(/|$) {
        try_files $uri =404;
        include fastcgi_params;
        fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name;
        fastcgi_param HTTPS $https;
        fastcgi_pass unix:/home/app/run/php-fpm.sock;
    }

    # every other address: the app
    location / {
        try_files $uri @rewrite;
    }
    location @rewrite {
        rewrite ^/(.+)$ /index.php last;
    }

    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload";
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
    add_header Referrer-Policy "origin";
}

The app sends its own Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options and Permissions-Policy headers with each page.

Behind a proxy or load balancer

NetFlow9 takes the client's address from the connection. If another proxy is in front of nginx, list its addresses in app.trusted_proxies (app/config.php). Its X-Forwarded-For is then believed for sign-in limits and the audit log.

Logs

The app writes to logs/: app.log, daemon.log, php_error.log, and nginx's access and error logs. Rotate them, for example with etc/logrotate-qsm-app (weekly, 3 kept, or at 100 MB).

pages.title: Daemon and services
pages.summary: The workflow daemon, the systemd services, and the command-line tools.
pages.html:
Runs started by triggers, schedules, waits, human task time limits and outgoing emails are queued as jobs. The daemon runs them. Without it, scheduled workflows don't start and emails aren't sent.

Installing the services

sudo scripts/4_services-install.sh install [--no-playwright]
scripts/4_services-install.sh status
sudo scripts/4_services-install.sh uninstall

It writes these systemd units, starts them, and enables them at boot:

UnitRuns
nfn-daemon.serviceThe workflow daemon (app/v.php daemon::run), as the app's user, logging to logs/daemon.log. Restarted if it fails.
nfn-haraka.serviceHaraka, for inbound mail, only when it is installed.
playwright-mcp.serviceThe web browser tool server, unless --no-playwright.

It also adds a polkit rule that lets the app's user start, stop and restart these units, so super-admins can manage them from the administration pages.

Note: polkit must be installed first (minimal systems leave it out: dnf install polkit). Without it, the script stops before writing anything.

The daemon's options

OptionDefaultDescription
--min-workers2Worker processes started at once and always kept.
--max-workers2 × CPUs − 1More workers are started while jobs wait. The extra ones stop after --idle-timeout (60 s) without work.
--max-per-accountmax − 1Running jobs of one account (0: no limit), so one account cannot take all workers.
--max-per-projectmax − 1Running jobs of one project (0: no limit).
--job-timeout0Seconds a job may run before its worker is killed (0: no limit).
--max-worker-memory256MB. A worker above it is replaced after its job.

A job whose worker dies or times out is queued again, and given up after 3 attempts. Given-up jobs appear in the account's execution log.

Command-line tools

Run them from app/ as the app's user, with ./v <command>:

CommandDoes
./v wf::run --id=<workflow>Starts and runs a workflow's draft.
./v wf::resume --id=<execution>Runs a sleeping execution again.
./v seed::indexesCreates the database indexes (after an upgrade).
./v audit::verify [--account=<id>]Checks the audit log's seal: changed, forged or missing entries.
./v tiers::show [--account=<id>], ./v tiers::setThe plans, and an account's plan, limits and usage.
./v Admin::admins::list | grant | revokeThe super-admins. See Administration.
./v SystemAI::credits::show | add | plan | ratesThe accounts' AI credits.
./v LocalMCP::servers::list | enable | disable | testThe tool servers and the accounts that may use them.
./v check::run [--only=…] [--verbose]The check suite (also commands/CheckCommand.sh).

pages.title: Inbound mail
pages.summary: Receiving email for the Email (inbound) trigger with Haraka: DNS, installation and configuration.
pages.html:
The Email (inbound) trigger needs the installation to receive email. NetFlow9 uses Haraka, a mail server on Node.js, with a NetFlow9 plugin. It accepts mail for the trigger addresses only, stores each message and starts its workflow. Without Haraka, the trigger and its settings page don't appear.

1. DNS

Choose a domain for the addresses, such as in.example.com, and point its MX record at the server. Port 25 must be open to the internet.

2. Install Haraka

The installer does steps 2 to 4 when you choose Inbound email (sudo ./install.sh in the app's folder; run it again to add it later). Alone, as root (Haraka's files stay the app's user's):

sudo scripts/2_haraka-install.sh --domain=in.example.com [--version=vX.Y.Z] [--dir=<folder>] [--dry-run]

It installs Haraka into <app>/haraka (or HARAKA_DIR), with the MongoDB driver, NetFlow9's plugin and configuration, then Haraka's defaults. It never overwrites what is already there.

3. Configure

  • In app.env, set MAIL_INBOUND_DOMAIN=in.example.com.
  • Haraka's MongoDB user: when MongoDB's users exist (Security), its connection string is in app.env (HARAKA_MONGO_URI) and the install writes it into haraka/config/nfn.ini. Otherwise set uri there yourself.
  • Create DKIM keys if you want them: cd haraka/dkim && ./dkim_key_gen.sh in.example.com, then publish the TXT record it writes in in.example.com/dns (more: haraka -h dkim).

4. Start it

sudo scripts/4_services-install.sh install

This adds nfn-haraka.service. Haraka runs as root to listen on port 25.

Addresses

Each Email (inbound) step gets an address <prefix>-<code>@in.example.com. The prefix is the account's, set by its owner under Settings → Inbound mail.

pages.title: System AI
pages.summary: Offering an AI model to every account, paid with credits: provider, model, credits and rates.
pages.html:
The System AI is an AI model your installation offers to every account, so they can use AI steps and the Assistant without their own API key. Their use is paid in credits: a monthly allowance per account, plus top-ups.

Turning it on

Set in app.env, then restart PHP-FPM and the daemon:

SYSTEM_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic
SYSTEM_AI_API_KEY='sk-ant-…'
SYSTEM_AI_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5
SYSTEM_AI_EFFORT=high
SYSTEM_AI_MONTHLY_CREDITS=500
SYSTEM_AI_MAX_CREDITS_PER_REQUEST=200

The provider can be anthropic, openai, gemini, ollama or lemonade. For a local server, set SYSTEM_AI_URL. For models other than Claude's, set SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_INPUT and SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_OUTPUT (USD per million tokens) so their use can be counted.

Then the AI steps of that provider list System AI as a credential, and the Assistant offers System AI as a provider.

Credits

  • Every account gets SYSTEM_AI_MONTHLY_CREDITS each month, or its plan's ai_monthly_credits. Unused credits don't roll over.
  • Top-ups add credits on top, valid for 12 months: ./v SystemAI::credits::add, or a super-admin from the account's administration page.
  • Each call counts its tokens in credits, by the model's rate. A run reserves credits first and stops before a call once they are used up.
  • The rates per model and the margin are in app/plugins/SystemAI/credit_rates.php. Copy it to credit_rates.local.php to change them.
./v SystemAI::credits::show --account=<id>
./v SystemAI::credits::add  --account=<id> …
./v SystemAI::credits::plan --account=<id> …
./v SystemAI::credits::rates

Accounts see their balance under Settings → AI credits.

pages.title: Tool servers
pages.summary: MCP servers the installation runs for the AI steps, such as a sandboxed web browser.
pages.html:
Tool servers are MCP servers that run on your installation and are offered to the AI steps of the accounts you choose. The first one is a web browser (Playwright, headless Chromium): the model can open pages, read them, click, type and fill in forms.

Installing the web browser

sudo scripts/1_playwright-install.sh        # Playwright and Chromium, for every user
sudo scripts/playwright-mcp.sh install      # the browser server, as a service

The browser server runs as its own user without a login, listens on 127.0.0.1:8931 only, and uses a fresh browser profile for each session. A firewall table stops it from reaching private, loopback and link-local addresses, including cloud metadata, so it reaches only the public internet.

Giving accounts access

./v LocalMCP::servers::test
./v LocalMCP::servers::enable  --account=<id> --server=playwright
./v LocalMCP::servers::disable --account=<id> --server=playwright
./v LocalMCP::servers::list

A super-admin can also switch servers on and off on the account's administration page. Enabled accounts see the server under Tool servers in their AI steps.

Configuration

The servers are listed in app/plugins/LocalMCP/servers.php (or your servers.local.php). For each server: its label and description, its MCP address, the tools the model may use (only the safe browser tools by default), and the most sessions at once in all (4) and per account (2).

pages.title: Administration
pages.summary: Super-admins: the installation's services, the accounts, plans and limits, suspending and viewing accounts.
pages.html:
An installation can host several accounts. Super-admins manage the installation and all accounts from Settings → Administration.

Super-admins

The super-admin flag is set only from the command line, never by a form:

./v Admin::admins::grant --email=ana@example.com [--account=<id>]
./v Admin::admins::list
./v Admin::admins::revoke --email=ana@example.com

Super-admins must use two-factor authentication to open the administration pages. Every action they take is recorded in the audit log of the account acted on, and in their own.

The installation

The Installation page shows the services (daemon, Haraka, browser) with their health, and lets you start, stop and restart them. It needs the systemd units of 4_services-install.sh. It also shows the System AI and the tool servers.

Accounts

The Accounts page lists the accounts with their plan, users, projects, workflows and runs of the last 30 days. Open one to:

  • Tier & limits: choose its plan, and change single limits or features for this account only.
  • Credits: its AI credits, plan and top-ups.
  • Tool servers: which ones it may use.
  • Suspend: its users are signed out at once, nothing new runs, and its queued jobs wait. Reactivate undoes it.
  • View as: see the account as its owner does, read-only and for a limited time, with a bar to go back.

Plans (tiers)

Plans set the limits and features of accounts. They are defined in app/tiers.php, or your tiers.local.php:

PlanData tablesRows per tableFilesAI credits / monthFeatures
Free31,000100 MB100none
Team50100,00010 GB2,000none
Enterpriseno limitno limitno limitthe installation'sSAML, LDAP sign-in

Accounts without a plan get the default plan, Enterprise in the shipped file. Change plans with the Tier & limits panel or ./v tiers::set.

Sign-up

With the Registration plugin enabled (app/plugins.php), the sign-in page has a link to sign up: people can create a new account themselves. Remove it from the list to turn sign-up off.

pages.title: Backups and upgrades
pages.summary: What to back up, how to restore, and how to upgrade NetFlow9.
pages.html:
What to back up

WhatWhy
The MongoDB databaseEverything: accounts, users, workflows, executions, credentials, data tables, and the files (stored in MongoDB GridFS). Use mongodump, or your MongoDB backup tooling.
